title: Brian Branch, 1 other Detroit Lions player fined for Packers game
summary: Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch was fined this week for a hit delivered to Green Bay Packers tight end Tucker Kraft. The fine was for “use of the helmet,” and carries a $23,882 fine. That is the standard amount of a penalty like this, as it was his first offense of the season—but far from […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive back Brian Branch (32) waves at fans to celebrate 20-17 win over Green Bay Packers at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch was fined this week for a hit delivered to Green Bay Packers tight end Tucker Kraft. The fine was for “use of the helmet,” and carries a $23,882 fine. That is the standard amount of a penalty like this, as it was his first offense of the season—but far from his first offense of this type. Here’s a look at Branch’s infraction: Hey @nfl can y'all do something about this??? pic.twitter.com/2CKGCkTsbS — Easton Butler (@Easton__Butler) October 25, 2026 Branch has a history of fines like this. According to Spotrac, Branch has been previously fined a total of 15 times , including five involving an impermissible use of his helmet and two hits on a defenseless receiver. He’s also been ejected/suspended twice: once for helmet-to-helmet hit against the Packers in 2024, and he was suspended for one week after throwing punches at Chiefs receiver JuJu Smith-Schuster after the game. This was just Branch’s first game back after suffering a torn Achilles in December last year. He played a limited role against the Packers, but Lions coach Dan Campbell noted on Friday he will have no pitch count in Sunday’s game against the Vikings. “Now he’s ready. So yes, there are no limitations on him going into this game,” Campbell said. Other Week 7 fine notes: Derrick Barnes was also fined for a late hit that was flagged in the game. No Lions players were fined for taunting despite their boisterous celebration following a Packers offsides penalty—but Packers cornerback Brandon Cisse was fined for taunting. There were no other fines from that Week 7 game.

full_text: WELCOME TO MOVEMBER! It’s time for our sixth annual Movember Charity Drive, where we raise money for charity for the entire month of November. In addition to raising money, we’ll also be giving away prizes, running an auction, and doing a bunch of silly and humiliating stuff over on our YouTube and Twitch live streams. Here’s everything you need to know about our 2026 Pride of Detroit Movember Charity Drive. Charities (two this year!) For the third straight year, we are again raising funds for the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center , specifically for their Men’s Cancer Research Fund. Voted the highest rated center for cancer care in Michigan by the U.S. News & World Report’s Best Hospital rankings, the Rogel Center is at the cutting edge of both cancer treatment and research. Donations collected through our fundraiser will go directly toward supporting groundbreaking research, raising awareness, and providing critical resources to patients in need. We are also representing a second charity, with fundraising happening exclusively through our auction. That charity is the House of Providence , Michigan-based intervention program that aides in helping kids in foster care with educational programs and other support systems until they can find a forever home. How to donate through our campaign If you want to donate to our campaign for the Rogel Cancer Center: Simple! Just head to our donation page here. To support our charity drive for the House of Providence, check out our auction section here (more information below). Direct donations to the House of Providence are always very appreciated, but those will not go towards our final total, as we have no way to track them. Donation rewards After Movember is over, I will email donors who have reached this level of donation (it can be through multiple donations, as long as they’re made under the same name/email ), and if you qualify, you can cash in for the following rewards: $100 — Subscription to POD Direct into preseason 2027 (If you’re already a subscriber, you can gift it!) $250 — Cameo-type personalized video of your choosing $500 (new this year!) — Private group Q&A with Erik and Jeremy $750 (new this year!) — POD 2028 calendar (more info below) $1,000 — Be a guest on the PODcast Donation incentives There are also individual rewards you can earn with a single donation. To redeem a donation incentive, please make sure to list your choice in your donation message. Here are the individual rewards you can earn automatically by donating (can only choose one with each donation): $25— Write word/short phrase on podcaster’s face $50— Mute podcast host of your choice for 1 minute $100— Change Jeremy’s green screen background $300 — Egg smashed on someone’s head $500 — Host will do a celebrity impression for at least 30 seconds (must be appropriate) Auction items Our auction is going to be a little different than in previous years, but way bigger and way better. Our friends at Encore Legacy Auctions are handling the auction this year, and they have HUNDREDS of items for several different sports teams available. Five percent of the winning bids will go to the House of Providence. In addition , we’ll have several Pride of Detroit exclusive items where 100% of the proceeds will go to House of Providence . That includes some experience-based auction items, including: Grab a drink with Jeremy and Erik Play a round of disc golf with Jeremy Have a virtual NFL Draft prospect film watching session with Erik We’ll also have some Detroit Lions swag that will be added to the auction later this month. Donation goals Last year, we raised over $32,000. This year, we’ve got loftier goals and even better incentives along the way. Here’s what will happen if we collectively hit some milestones: $5,000 — Activates PODcast host punishment by Lions (see below) $10,000 — POD team runs a 5k $15,000 — POD staff has to reveal high school photos $20,000 — JCPenney-style photoshoot, resulting in a POD calendar (available for $750 donation) $25,000 — POD team does public karaoke of Toto’s “Africa” $30,000 — Jeremy learns and records a TikTok dance $35,000 — Jeremy reveals a comedy sketch from his past $40,000 — Jeremy gets frosted tips, a la Skyler Gill-Howard $45,000 — Ryan reveals college poetry $50,000 — Erik watches a 15-minute Aaron Rodgers highlight reel with “I <3 Aaron” shirt $60,000 — Jeremy dresses up like Marilyn Monroe $75,000 — Jeremy will grow out his hair for an entire year Once we hit $5,000, it will activate a new challenge that we will try to accomplish at the end of the month, based on how the Detroit Lions perform in the entire month of November (five games). Here’s how it works: For Jeremy: For every 15+ yard pass interference penalty in a Lions game, Jeremy will do 10 pushups For Ryan: For every Jared Goff TD, Ryan will review a track from Kid Rock’s new album and post it For Meko: For every Sione Vaki gain of 10+ yards, Meko will run a mile Wheel of pain For every $1,000 that we raise, we’ll spin what we endearingly call the Wheel of Pain. title: Minnesota Vikings vs. Detroit Lions preview: 5 small weaknesses in Vikings defense
summary: Riding a two-game winning streak, the Detroit Lions have a massive home-field opportunity to knock the NFL’s last remaining undefeated team off its warship throne, move within striking distance of first place in the NFC North, and exact revenge for last year’s two defeats to the Vikings, both highly uncharacteristic of the team’s identity under […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 02: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) leaps high for a catch during the Detroit Lions versus the Minnesota Vikings game on Sunday November 2, 2025 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Riding a two-game winning streak, the Detroit Lions have a massive home-field opportunity to knock the NFL’s last remaining undefeated team off its warship throne, move within striking distance of first place in the NFC North, and exact revenge for last year’s two defeats to the Vikings, both highly uncharacteristic of the team’s identity under Dan Campbell. Prior to last season, Campbell had won five straight games against Kevin O’Connell, including four in a row with Brian Flores as defensive coordinator. The Lions’ quest to regain the throne of the North will ride on the shoulders of their All-Pro-caliber backfield duo of Jared Goff and Jahmyr Gibbs, and an offense facing a Vikings defense under Flores that is off to a historically lethal start, pillaging opponents on its way to a 6-0 record (11 wins straight dating back to last season). With the stakes incredibly high for Halloween weekend, this week’s preview dives into the cranium of Detroit’s Megamind, Drew Petzing, as he squares off against not just Flores but his former quarterback, Kyler Murray. We’ll examine how the Lions’ offense can keep the monsters from underneath their bed. Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus. The Trojan Norse The Minnesota Vikings’ pass defense, with its 70.0%+ blitz rate, has been nightmare fuel for opposing quarterbacks. They lead the league in EPA/dropback allowed (-0.323), success rate allowed (38.2%), sack rate (10.1%), and pressure rate (38.6%). The Vikings’ unpredictable, overwhelming, exotic blitzes have tricked offenses so thoroughly that teams are frightened to run play-action passes, worried that quarterbacks momentarily turning their backs to the defense to sell the run fake could hinder their processing and lead to immediate negative plays. Teams are averaging only a 19.3% play-action pass rate against Minnesota (31st), totaling just 40 such dropbacks. The Packers had 10 play-action dropbacks in Week 1 against the Vikings, and no offense has exceeded that total in a game since. The Saints and Colts combined for only six play-action dropbacks over the last two weeks. Meanwhile, the Lions’ offense ranks fourth this season with a 33.3% play-action pass rate and has recorded at least 11 such dropbacks in every game. Against play-action passes this season, the Vikings’ defense is allowing 7.9 yards per attempt (19th), +0.003 EPA/dropback (12th), a 48.3% success rate (11th), and a staggering 13.8% explosive pass rate (27th). The inherent risk of turning your back to Minnesota’s defense and becoming the Headless Hurler is still real, as the Vikings have recorded a 16.2% sack rate (1st) and 48.6% pressure rate (1st) against play-action dropbacks. The Vikings haven’t quite been tested against play action this season, with their matchup against the Bears coming in a monsoon, hardly a fair test of their passing attack. They’ll also face the Bills next week, an offense with the league’s second-highest play-action rate. While Minnesota remains formidable against play action, particularly with its ability to generate pressure and sacks, its defense ranks outside the top 10 in several metrics. It hasn’t been nearly as historically dominant against play action as it has against the run and on traditional dropbacks. As Petzing illuminated last week, and as Lions fans have witnessed for years, Jared Goff is a different breed of beast as a precision processor when it comes to play-action passing . Detroit’s offensive line is also above average in pass protection, with room to improve as its younger players develop and the heady Cade Mays continues acclimating at the pivot. Now it’s a matter of proving they aren’t afraid of the dark when facing Minnesota’s pressure packages and are willing to challenge the Vikings with the play-action passing game that has been a staple of Detroit’s offense. The Devil’s in the Dropback Continuing on the topic of counterpunches to the Vikings flooding pass-rush lanes with second-level defenders such as Eric Wilson, Blake Cashman, the immortal Harrison Smith, and Josh Metellus. There’s another potential wrinkle for Detroit’s offense. It’s not often the Vikings are forced to defend straight dropbacks from under center. No team really is in this era of the NFL, but the Lions could be equipped to do it. The Lions are averaging only 1.8 such dropbacks per game this season, but Jared Goff has completed 6-of-9 passes (66.7% completion percentage, 6th) for 84 yards (9.3 yards per attempt, 3rd) and two touchdowns (t-2nd). Detroit also ranks in the top 10 in success rate and explosive pass rate on under-center straight dropbacks, while its 4.7 yards after catch per attempt ranks fourth. They do need to be careful, however, as they’ve allowed a 40.0% quarterback pressure rate (7th) and one sack on these plays. Luckily, straight dropbacks from under center have helped disarm the Vikings a bit. Flores’ furious, fully fanged forces have faced 15 under-center, non-play-action dropbacks this season (10th), allowing opponents to complete 9-of-14 passes (64.3% completion percentage, 6th) for 132 yards (9.4 yards per attempt)—nearly a first down per pass attempt, albeit on a small sample size! Minnesota also ranks in the bottom 10 in success rate and explosive pass rate allowed on these plays. Perhaps most surprisingly, they’ve generated pressure on just 13.3% of those dropbacks (t-27th). The real treat is that the Vikings’ defense is allowing a league-worst 6.4 yards after catch per attempt on such passes. Perhaps all those aggressive, mugged-up looks at the line of scrimmage are proving hazardous, with defenders scrambling to get into coverage position after the snap and missing tackles. This preview is about finding the small levers the Lions’ offense can pull against the most dangerous defense in the league. The Vikings’ pass defense feels inevitable. Stay on the field long enough, and they’ll get you. They’ll force you into mistakes. Just like with play-action passes, straight dropbacks from under center offer a small avenue to exploit Minnesota’s aggression, get its defenders on their heels, and produce chunk plays. It’s an opportunity to move downfield quickly, catch Flores’ defense with its pants down, and get the ball into the hands of Detroit’s best playmakers with room to operate. Ragnarök Meets Rah Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown can be a ghoul to opposing defenses. It’s part of why he’s a three-time consecutive All-Pro, and his hands, toughness, and consistency have helped him slay the Vikings in the past. Over his last six games against the Vikings, St. Brown has averaged 10.8 targets, 8.3 receptions, 100.7 receiving yards, 0.5 touchdowns, and 5.1 first downs per game. That production is more menacingly consistent than Michael Myers terrorizing Haddonfield, Illinois. And as much as everyone loves Dr. Loomis, Flores might as well be playing his role, desperately trying and repeatedly failing to contain the Michael Myers of Detroit’s offense. Against the blitz this season, St. Brown has recorded 25 targets, 16 receptions, 204 receiving yards, three touchdowns, and 70 yards after catch. All five rank in the top 10 among wide receivers against the blitz. He’s been a ball magnet for Jared Goff when defenses bring extra rushers. Last season, St. Brown was targeted 61 times against the blitz, hauling in 39 receptions (2nd) for 593 receiving yards (2nd), four touchdowns, and 329 yards after catch (1st). The Sun God has been Detroit’s secret weapon against the blitzkrieg. As a secondary sidekick, while Sam LaPorta hasn’t experienced…

title: The Packers can’t run block
summary: Stating the complete obvious, but the Green Bay Packers’ running game has reached a level of hopelessness that seems almost statistically impossible. Coming into Thursday night, the Carolina Panthers ranked a paltry 30th in EPA allowed per rush. If there was ever going to be any sort of “get right” game for the offensive line, […]
full_text: (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Stating the complete obvious, but the Green Bay Packers’ running game has reached a level of hopelessness that seems almost statistically impossible. Coming into Thursday night, the Carolina Panthers ranked a paltry 30th in EPA allowed per rush. If there was ever going to be any sort of “get right” game for the offensive line, it was going to happen against Carolina. They had just been pummeled by Tampa Bay four days earlier, facing 48 carries and allowing a 94th percentile rushing success rate to the Buccaneers. They were tired, they were on the road, and they are a bad run defense. And it didn’t matter. Despite starting left guard Aaron Banks returning to the lineup last night, he struggled more than anyone else. In watching all of the Packers’ 25 running back carries, I credited Banks with seven errors or lost blocks that lead to the play not working as intended (either leading to the tackle or disrupting the intended play design). That’s a rate of 28%. His fellow guard Laken Tomlinson, playing on the right side now after Banks’ return, was credited with four errors. Emergency third-string center John Williams was credited with three, including a really bad whiff near the goal line. Josh Jacobs somehow scored on this but good grief John Williams whiffed hard pic.twitter.com/K57xfSxaqF — rcon14 (@rcon14) October 30, 2026 The tackles were better, with Belton credited for two, and Morgan’s only error involving missing the linebacker on the Jacobs toss to the left. Bo Melton managed to make two errors in a matter of three plays on the final drive, both missing his crack block (bad) and getting thrown four yards into the backfield against a defensive end (understandable for the small receiver). Of the 25 carries the Packers’ running backs had, I counted a whopping six carries where someone didn’t mess something up. The running game generally requires everyone to do their job to generate positive plays, and if you always have someone messing up, you just can’t get those four, five, or six-yard gains that you need to reliably sustain drives on the ground. The problem wasn’t entirely isolated to the offensive line, though, even if they were the primary culprit. We also had this vision masterpiece from Marshawn Lloyd. i'm going to become the joker pic.twitter.com/XxZ3mEKG0w — rcon14 (@rcon14) October 30, 2026 I think stopping your feet because there's a safety fifteen yards away from you while your OL and TE blocked this thing up perfectly is a new low in the Marshawn Lloyd is a blind bat commentary pic.twitter.com/F9g2l0S2tA — rcon14 (@rcon14) October 30, 2026 This may actually be the best blocked play of the entire game and Lloyd somehow manages to screw it up despite this being exactly where he is supposed to run. ffs bro this is where you are supposed to go you are looking directly at it!!! pic.twitter.com/lrL8P9adId — rcon14 (@rcon14) October 30, 2026 Between Lloyd’s vision problems and Josh Jacobs’ complete lack of juice running the ball, the Packers got basically nothing out of their running back room even in the rare instances that things were blocked up relatively well. The Packers run game had 1.6 yards after contact per attempt in Week 8 against the Panthers That is the lowest number for any winning team this season, per @SumerSports — Shawn Syed (@SyedSchemes) October 30, 2026 Both Jacobs and Lloyd are over one yard worse than expected per carry this season, with Lloyd ranking dead last amongst qualified rushers by a truly incredible .4 yards per carry. Josh Jacobs’ number? It would rank second-worst in the NFL if he had enough carries to qualify. The Packers can’t block, and when they do block, they can’t capitalize on it because the running backs either can’t see the hole, are too slow to leverage the advantage, or go down shortly after first contact. Matt LaFleur seems to be reaching a loss in how to get the run game going too. LaFleur on belief in the run game. pic.twitter.com/8Yx4dI3YqO — Bill Huber (@BillHuberNFL) October 30, 2026 And I can’t blame him. Even if the Packers bring Kevin Zeitler into the fold, that’s only one spot potentially improving. While Laken Tomlinson has been a godsend in comparison to Jacob Monk, Donovan Jennings, and Jager Burton, he’s still been extremely limited in the run game. Aaron Banks just played one of his worst career games in both the run and passing game. John Williams is holding his own, but no one is confusing him for a good center. When your best run blockers are Jordan Morgan and Anthony Belton, there’s only so much you can do. And that’s before you have running backs actively harming the run game. There’s nowhere left to run. Quite literally.

title: Packers Film Room: Long snapping on kicks in Week 8
summary: In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We’ve got 4 this week, all of the extra point variety. Listen. Between you, me, the fencepost and our little stick figure friend, I started this article in the preseason because everyone seemed to have long-snapper takes and I wanted […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We’ve got 4 this week, all of the extra point variety. Listen. Between you, me, the fencepost and our little stick figure friend, I started this article in the preseason because everyone seemed to have long-snapper takes and I wanted to try to at least have an informed take. I thought it would be a silly little article that I could write quickly every week, learn a little and get on with my life. With the struggles of Smack, I’ve seen more long snapper takes each and every week, and every week this takes a little bit more of my life. It’s been great. Sometimes I wish it didn’t take quite so much time & energy, but I love it dearly and have learned a ton. I’m still just scratching the surface here, but I feel like we’re doing something pretty fun here. Alright. How does our charting look this week? Rough day for snapping this week. Easily Orzech’s worst performance. For the record, I don’t think Whelan is actually mad like the stick figure suggests, but I told Ryan at Pride of Detroit that I’d try to work in some angry eyebrows if given the opportunity. So here ya go, buddy. Kick 1: Extra Point Miss Good snap, over the hold point with the spin on the snap allowing Whelan to catch it by the laces and get it down for a good hold. Based on the flags there is very little wind, so the hold of Whelan is tilted slightly forward and away from Smack. The snap-to-kick timing was 1.3 seconds, which is exactly what you want. Watching this live, I thought it could have been blocked, but that was not the case. It’s a low trajectory kick and he just kinda yanks it. As the stick figure suggests – and as we will see – this was not a good day overall from Orzech, but the lone miss on the day was not on him. Side note: I watched this game at a local sports bar with my brothers (the wings were good last night). When the ball hit the uprights, we heard a glass-shattering noise at the moment of impact, and we weren’t sure if someone dropped a tray or if it was from the broadcast. Apparently it was from the broadcast. Either the uprights sound like shattered glass when they’re hit or something happened near a mic at the same moment the ball hit the upright. Kick 2: Extra Point Make High snap from Orzech. Not over Whelan’s head, but at his face, to the point where Whelan has to adjust to the catch. Whelan is able to make the catch and get down a nice hold down for a snap-to-kick time of 1.35 seconds. Kick 3: Extra Point Make Good snap to the body, good hold, good kick. Nothing major to say here. Solid operation. Kick 4: Extra Point Make The snap is low. It’s to the location of the hold point, but it’s on the ground when it arrives to Whelan. As commenter Wedge-31 has pointed out, this is a tough position for the snap, as it causes the holder to have to lean forward to adjust to the snap, then rock back while getting the hold down. This doesn’t interrupt the kicking process, because Whelan’s a pro. Smack keeps his timing and the kick-to-snap timing is at a crisp 1.3 seconds. Albums listened to: Nine Inch Nails – The Fragile

title: Weekend Musings: Mid-term report for the Houston Texans
summary: Few seasons in the 25-year history of the franchise opened with as much anticipation and expectation as this season did for the Houston Texans. Coming off a season that tied the franchise record for wins (12) and its third straight season with a trip to the divisional round, Houston seemingly built a foundation for bigger […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 04: C.J. Stroud #7 of the Houston Texans takes the field prior to a game against the Dallas Cowboys at Reliant Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images Few seasons in the 25-year history of the franchise opened with as much anticipation and expectation as this season did for the Houston Texans. Coming off a season that tied the franchise record for wins (12) and its third straight season with a trip to the divisional round, Houston seemingly built a foundation for bigger and better things. That the squad practically returned all its key defensive starters only added to the expectations. Free agency and the draft addressed the biggest weaknesses of the squad, mainly the offensive line and the running game. The team added reinforcements to the defense with the free agent signing of Reed Blankenship and drafting of All-American DL MacDonald. All reasons for optimism. Once the regular season started…the optimism, uh, didn’t last. Houston sits at 2-5, 2-3 in the conference and 2-1 in the division. They are an alarming 0-4 at home. Penalties are still a major concern fours years into the Ryans regime, and he faces the most negative press of his career. Nick Caley is still on many fans “fire into the sun” list, but perhaps the worst coach award has been between DC Matt Burke and DB coach Dino Vasso. The team is getting picked apart through the air, and too often you see defenders confused about coverage schemes/assignments. OFFENSE: C Coming into the season, if Houston struggled, you figured it because of the continued struggles of CJ Stroud. His 2025-26 playoff performance stunned most. While his draft-mate Will Anderson Jr. got the big second contract, Stroud just got the 5th year option pick-up. As of now, Stroud is putting much of the negative press behind him. The Texans are 8th in total passing yards, with Stroud 5th in passing, with only three turnovers against him (2 of those came in the first game against Buffalo). WR Nico Collins is still Stroud’s primary offensive weapon. When he missed two games due to injury, the offense could only generate 2 total TDs. 2nd-year receiver Jaylin Noel was having a breakout season but suffered a season-ending injury against the Giants. Dalton Schultz is still a solid receiving TE, but the rest of the receiving corps, to include newly acquired Marvin Harrison Jr are mostly just…there. As for the previously maligned running game…it is not better. Aside from the opener against a porous Bills defense and the London game against Jacksonville, the team struggled to rush for more than 80 total yards/game. David Montgomery, outside of his 3 total touchdown effort in Week 1, has offered nothing of significance and missed two games due to injury. Woody Marks resumed the RB1 role, but he, nor any other back on the roster, has rushed for more than 66 yards in a game, and the squad’s longest single run on the season is 25 yards. The offense line has not been particularly effective in run-blocking, with the pass-blocking only slightly better. Play-calling consistency and philosophy are also up for debate. Remember the talk about 12 formations? Houston is using them, but they can’t quit the heavy formations with the extra O-lineman, with less-than-ideal results. Offensive MVP: QB CJ Stroud. He is the one constant on the offense. While not perfect, he has put Houston in position to win almost all of its games, leading the team to take a late 4th quarter lead or tie in 6 of the 7 games played. Also considered: WR Nico Collins, WR Jaylin Noel Offensive LVP: G Wyatt Teller. Signed to offer competition for the starting line, he slated into the RG slot when Ed Ingram went out with injury. His performance has not been…quality. Especially in run-blocking, which is a critical evaluation point for that position, Teller hasn’t lived up to his (relatively) modest contract. Not that Ingram has lit up the running game when he’s been in, but if Ingram is out and Teller has to play, don’t expect a lot of goodness to come from that side of the line. Really, the entire run-blocking scheme is up for debate. Also considered: RB David Montgomery DEFENSE: D- Usually, strengths quickly devolving into weaknesses only happen in comics and politics. Consider the Texans’ defense. They were #1 in yards allowed, #2 in points allowed and generally atop almost all defensive metrics in 2025. In 2026, not so much. In particular, the pass defense, which was #6 in pass yards allowed in 2025, now ranks 27th. In explosive plays allowed, the team is second-worst. Secondary players have only 2 INTs (3 total for the team), far off the pace for 17 INTs (19 team total) they set last season. At least until the Giants game, the run defense was solid. The defensive line is a mixed bag, for while Anderson and Hunter still bring the pressure (11.5 combined sacks/15.5 TFLs), the rest of the line has been so-so. The LB unit is fighting injuries and inconsistency. However, the secondary is most hurting the squad. Between regression, injuries and poor communication, this secondary reminds fans more of the 2010 defense vs. the lockdown-unit of 2025. Defensive MVP: Will Anderson, Jr. 33 Total Tackles (17 Solo)/7.5 sacks/11.5 TFLs/1 FF/1 FR. If there were worries about falling off after securing his $50M/year contract, those are no longer a concern. Defensive LVP: CB Kamari Lassiter. Last season, you could’ve called Lassiter the best CB2 in the league. This season, he is more a coverage liability. In addition to hurting the team defense, this performance is likely costing him a lot of money, as he approaches eligibility for a contract extension. Also considered: S Reed Blankenship, who is continuing the trend of ex-Philly safeties playing poorly once in Houston. SPECIAL TEAMS: C+/B- Frank Ross’ units generally rank in the top tier of special teams categories. However, this season, that has been inconsistent. The kick return coverage does not always reward the squad for forcing kickoffs, as seen with Indy, Dallas and Jacksonville. Ka’imi Fairbairn is playing to his usually solid level for FGs, save a meh game against Cincinnati. His kickoff capabilities have been a little more mercurial. The punting unit is solid, but not spectacular. Brinkman had a bad snap against the Bengals when Houston missed that early FG. The return units haven’t been all that special, although Noel before his injury did have his moments. Perhaps Tank Dell can step back into being a dangerous returner, especially on punts. Special Teams MVP: PK Ka’imi Fairbairn. Improving on kick-offs and his placekicking is consistent. Also considered: Jaylin Noel. Special Teams LVP: No obvious candidate here. BEST WIN: 34-31 over Jacksonville in London. Only had two to choose from, so may as well go with the one over an opponent with a pulse. WORSE LOSS: 19-17 at Indianapolis. No shortage of options. Given the fire-sale of players going on with the Colts, losing to them like they did may really come back to hurt the Texans on so many levels. Also considered: 34-30 loss to the Cowboys, ’cause…Dallas. KEY PLAY (SO FAR): Week 1, 2:10, 2nd Qtr, BUF Ball @ BUF 4, Josh Allen 38-yard pass to TE Dalton Kincaid to BUF 42 . Not a play highlighted in the TDATDA archives. However, when Josh Allen, long victimized at NRG/Reliant, somehow landed a [KITTEN]-It ball deep to TE Kincaid with All-Pro Derek Stingley Jr. on the coverage, it set the tone for the team’s not just for that game, but for the first part of the season for the Texans. Last season, that is a play that Houston would pick off or at least force as an incompletion. Also considered: Week 4, 6:59, 3rd Qtr, DAL ball at the HOU 4, 4th and Goal: Prescott pass incomplete. Penalty on Lassiter (Defensive Holding) OVERALL MID-SEASON MVP: QB CJ Stroud. So far, when Houston succeeds, it is due to the offense, thus, the best player wins here. Also considered: DE Will Anderson, Jr. OVERALL MID-SEASON…

summary: This year’s Halloween is now just behind us, but there’s no question that playing the Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) (-7.5) in Duval County, Florida, has been nothing short of a personal ‘House of Horrors’ for the Indianapolis Colts (2-5), who haven’t won there since September 21, 2014. full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - OCTOBER 15: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts runs the ball during an NFL game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Field on October 15, 2023 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images This year’s Halloween is now just behind us, but there’s no question that playing the Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) (-7.5) in Duval County, Florida, has been nothing short of a personal ‘House of Horrors’ for the Indianapolis Colts (2-5), who haven’t won there since September 21, 2014. With the Colts jumpstarting their rebuild by trading two of their best veteran players earlier in the week: DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson, that sorry franchise streak doesn’t necessarily expect to change today going up against the AFC South’s leading team on the road. Kickoff is at 1 PM EST. For those Colts fans looking to watch, it’ll be aired on CBS with Spero Dedes (play-by-play), Adam Archuleta (analyst), and Aditi Kinkhabwala (sideline). The TV map can be found here . Meanwhile, for those tuning it, it can be listened to on 93.5 and 107.5 The Fan and 97.1 Hank FM locally. Per usual, Matt Taylor (play-by-play), Charles Arbuckle (analyst), and Larra Overton (sideline) will be on the call. Regarding those Sirius XM national radio subscribers, Colts fans can listen in on Channel 265 (car radio) and Channel 813 (Sirius XM app). The Colts come in with the league’s 20th highest scoring offense (22.0 avg. ppg.) while surrendering the 23rd most points (at 25.7 avg. ppg.) respectively. On the other hand, the Jaguars have the NFL’s 8th highest scoring offense (25.7 avg. ppg.) and allow the NFL’s 3rd fewest points defensively (17.3 avg. ppg) respectively. At EverBank Stadium, it’s expected to be around 77 to 78 degrees with scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms during game time. The officiating unit will be lead official Adrian Hill and his crew. Indianapolis leads the all-time series 28-22-0, but the Jaguars earned the most recent victory, beating the Colts 23-17 at Lucas Oil Stadium on December 28, 2025. Colts Injury Report: LB Bryce Boettcher (groin)- Questionable, WR Anthony Gould (concussion)- Out; TE Drew Ogletree (knee)- Questionable; and CB Justin Walley (knee)- Out. Jaguars Injury Report: S Antonio Johnson (ankle)- Out and WR Jakobi Meyers (hamstring/ankle)-Questionable.

title: 5 Questions with Big Cat Country: A New Era?
summary: In Week 8 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will travel to the sunshine state to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars. Knowing the party was hitting the road, I sat down with Gus Logue of Big Cat Country. We swapped questions and answers about both the Jaguars and Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 07: Tim Patrick #17 of the Jacksonville Jaguars makes a catch for a touchdown defended by Jaylon Jones #40 of the Indianapolis Colts during the second quarter at EverBank Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 8 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will travel to the sunshine state to take on the Jacksonville Jaguars. Knowing the party was hitting the road, I sat down with Gus Logue of Big Cat Country . We swapped questions and answers about both the Jaguars and Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned about this week’s enemy. You can find my answers to his questions here. Chris Shepherd: How are Jaguars fans feeling about their postseason chances sitting at 4-2 with a firm lead on the AFC South? Is this team a contender or do they just play in the AFCS? Gus Logue: I don’t think opinions in Jacksonville have changed much since before the season began. Of course, playing in the AFC South is a nice boost, but the Jaguars are clearly a top-10 or so team in the NFL right now. We’re just not yet sure whether this roster has hit its ceiling, which is a good thing, but one thing that could hold Jacksonville back from being a legitimate Super Bowl contender is its trench play. LT Anton Harrison was just lost for the season due to a knee injury, and every Jags fan is clamoring for pass rush help before the trade deadline. If the OL and DL can take a jump over the second half of the season, the league should really watch out for Jacksonville — and even if that doesn’t happen, Trevor Lawrence and Travis Hunter could still take this team far. Chris Shepherd: If you were an offensive coordinator tasked with creating a game plan to beat this Jaguars defense, what would it look like? Anyone you would target? Anyone you would avoid? Gus Logue: I would target the safety position in general. Antonio Johnson is quietly among Jacksonville’s best defensive players, but he’s been ruled out for Sunday’s game with an ankle injury. No. 2 safety Eric Murray had a concussion a few weeks ago and No. 3 safety Caleb Ransaw is on injured reserve. Very few rushers have been able to reach the second level of Jacksonville’s run defense, so in order to attack this undermanned secondary, I would put the ball in my quarterback’s hands and have him attack the middle of the field. Just don’t throw it to #12. Chris Shepherd: Who are a couple of lesser known players Colts fans should get ready to see a lot of this Sunday? Gus Logue: Rookie receiver Josh Cameron has been impressive in limited action thus far this season. Even if Brian Thomas Jr. does not get traded, expect the Jaguars to keep giving Cameron offensive snaps. The Baylor product has been a great glue guy with special teams and run blocking contributions, but he’s also super exciting with the ball in his hands. If you don’t know what folks mean when they say a wideout has “strong hands,” then watch Cameron. Kaevon Merriweather and Rayuan Lane III figure to split snaps at safety in Johnson’s absence, but I would also look for cornerback Montaric “Buster” Brown. He parlayed a career season into a new contract early in the offseason, but a hamstring injury has made him look almost unrecognizable. Jags fans will be praying that he is fully recovered coming out of the bye week. Chris Shepherd: Given a win this weekend Jacksonville will go to 5-2. Do you see a potential for them to make any moves at the trade deadline? What positions might they look to upgrade? Gus Logue: Perhaps they will add depth at offensive tackle after losing Harrison for the season. The more likely scenario is that Jacksonville upgrades its pass defense. The Jaguars have lacked pass rush depth since 2018 (only one year after its historic “Sacksonville” season). For years, the EDGE room has consisted of Josh Hines-Allen, Travon Walker, and a bunch of chumps. And Arik Armstead has been a decent 3-tech but interior push has been lacking for nearly a decade as well. The Jaguars need another pass rusher (Josh Sweat?) to help close out games against elite quarterbacks in January. But I also think that a veteran safety (Jessie Bates?) could fix a lot of communication errors in the secondary, the way Jakobi Meyers stabilized the passing offense last season. Chris Shepherd: The Jaguars are heavy favorites at home this weekend. How do you see this one playing out and what will the final score be? Gus Logue: I see the Jaguars taking care of business and winning by double-digit points. Let’s say 26-13. This is a potential look-ahead spot for Jacksonville, as they will play on Thursday Night Football in Baltimore next week, but they’ll be eager to play at home in new uniforms against a struggling division opponent on Sunday. The Bhayshul Tuten Breakout Game could come this week. And with that, ladies and gentlemen, our week eight preview with the enemy is in the books. I want to thank Gus Logue for giving us some answers to out questions for this week. Here’s to an entertaining and injury free game. As always, go Colts.
author: Chris Shepherd

title: Colts RB Jonathan Taylor reportedly available but would take ‘premium’ to move him
summary: According to NFL Insider Tom Pelissero in ‘The Sweep,’ Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor is available via trade, but it would take a significant draft capital haul for the franchise to part with its last remaining key veteran pillar: Colts RB Jonathan Taylor: How expensive would it be to get Taylor out of […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts looks on prior to the start of the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to NFL Insider Tom Pelissero in ‘The Sweep,’ Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor is available via trade, but it would take a significant draft capital haul for the franchise to part with its last remaining key veteran pillar : Colts RB Jonathan Taylor: How expensive would it be to get Taylor out of Indianapolis? The Colts have already been offered a 2027 second-round draft pick plus an additional pick for Taylor—and they immediately rejected it. Even after trading Nelson and Buckner, the Colts aren’t in fire sale mode. Taylor is only 27, he is the face of the franchise, and he just signed a two-year, $44 million contract extension in August. The Colts won’t deal him for anything other than a premium haul—and rightfully so. The Colts haven’t told other teams exactly what they want for Taylor, but it makes sense they’d want something close to deal the Panthers got when they traded Christian McCaffrey to San Francisco in 2022 in exchange for 2023 second-, third-, and fourth-round picks plus a 2024 fifth-rounder. Taylor is due about $4.866 million for the rest of this season, including active roster bonuses. His $15 million base salary for 2027 becomes fully guaranteed five days after the Super Bowl. The Colts reportedly were quick to turn down overtures of a second round pick, as Indianapolis appears to be holding out hope for at least a first round pick to part with their star workhorse during a busy week for the franchise, which already saw the Horseshoe trade fellow veterans Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. It’s already been reported that Colts team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon, who met with Taylor earlier this week, considers him potentially a major piece of the ongoing rebuild that was recently jumpstarted after such a disappointing start to Indianapolis’ season (at 2-5), that also saw longtime general manager Chris Ballard, the NFL executive who traded for and drafted Taylor back in the 2nd round of the 2020 NFL Draft, recently fired. Per ESPN’s Stephen Holder and longtime CBS 4/FOX 59’s Mike Chappell, while the Colts are currently listening on offers for Taylor from prospective trade suitors, Indianapolis isn’t actively shopping the franchise’s 2nd all-time career rushing leader (8,185) and all-time rushing touchdowns leader (77) either: One other point on Jonathan Taylor: There is a difference between shopping a player and taking calls. I would not describe what the Colts are doing as “shopping” JT. Might just be semantics but I thought it was worth mentioning. — Stephen Holder (@HolderStephen) October 31, 2026 JT and trade speculation. From everything I know and I’m out there all the time, of course the Colts are taking calls on JT availability/compensation. I don’t get the idea at all they are reaching out. They don’t need to and I believe Carlie wants JT to be part of rebuild. But if… — Mike Chappell (@mchappell51) October 31, 2026 On the season, Taylor has 140 carries for 587 total rushing yards (4.2 ypc. avg.) and 8 rushing touchdowns during all 7 starts. The expectation remains that if Taylor is still on the team, he’ll be active for Sunday’s game on the road against the Jacksonville Jaguars, per usual. Among suitors, there’s been reports that the Cincinnati Bengals, Denver Broncos, Green Bay Packers, Minnesota Vikings, New England Patriots, and New York Giants are among the teams that have already called and expressed interest in Taylor to the Colts regarding various degrees. However, again, the Colts have to be “blown away” by an offer, which likely means at least a first round pick to help Indianapolis get back into ‘Day 1,’ having also traded their 2027 first for Sauce Gardner in a premium package ahead of last year’s trade deadline. It’s a fair question though whether Indianapolis should seriously consider trading Taylor now to maximize the possible draft capital return, given that he is 27-years-old, has heavy mileage on his tires, and running backs don’t tend to age all that gracefully entering their thirties (unless you’re Derrick Henry and very few others). Meaning Taylor may only have 2-3 peak years left, which is realistically the amount of total time that it will take the Colts to fully complete a successful rebuild—that is, if all goes according to their next plan.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: The price for Jonathan Taylor: 1st round pick + Defensive Tackle
summary: The Colts are listening to offers for star Running Back Jonathan Taylor, despite him not requesting a trade like other Colts mid-2026 season. The Colts are reportedly valuing Taylor highly and there is a strong market for the 2025 NFL leader in Total Touchdowns from scrimmage, as teams look for him to be a final […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts carries the ball for a touchdown against the Minnesota Vikings during the first quarter of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts are listening to offers for star Running Back Jonathan Taylor, despite him not requesting a trade like other Colts mid-2026 season. The Colts are reportedly valuing Taylor highly and there is a strong market for the 2025 NFL leader in Total Touchdowns from scrimmage, as teams look for him to be a final piece for a deep playoff run. However, they are more than willing to keep Jonathan Taylor if no trade offer appeals to them. Of the offers they’ve already received, per The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero’s reported what isn’t enough to get the Colts to move on from their best Offensive player. The Colts already turned down a 2027 second-round draft pick plus an additional pick for RB Jonathan Taylor, making clear they’d want a premium to trade the face of the franchise. All the trade updates you can handle in The Sweep Insider Notebook: https://t.co/2eiMVV6AJ1 pic.twitter.com/FDIrQ5k9gc — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) October 31, 2026 A 2nd and another pick gets you hung up on. The Colts want a strong haul for Jonathan Taylor to trade him away before he breaks their franchise all time rushing yard record set by Hall of Famer Edgerrin James. Per journalist Josina Anderson of Exhibit News Network (formerly with CBS, ESPN, Fox, and Showtime), the Colts have named a price. The #Colts are not “now” open to trading RB Jonathan Taylor. 🙄 A desire for a 1st-rounder and a defensive tackle was discussed as of earlier this week… Read more below…. https://t.co/zCWbcTU8bM — JosinaAnderson (@JosinaAnderson) October 31, 2026 The Colts want a Round 1 pick (2027 or 2028, hasn’t been specified) as well as a defensive tackle. With DeForest Buckner a 49er once again, Grover Stewart over 33 years old and on an expiring deal, and Adetomiwa Adebawore on an expiring deal (albeit he is a priority re-sign according to the Colts), it makes sense the Colts would want to address the interior of their defensive front in their biggest potential trade before the deadline. With the list of suitors longer than a CVS receipt, there are a lot of different players (along with different draft pick packages) the Colts could net. Entering in a rebuild and previously prioritizing trading away expiring veteran contracts (Buckner and Quenton Nelson, the Colts will most likely prioritize young Defensive Tackles still on rookie contracts that could be promising additions to add to a developing core. Josina frames this from Colts view… not what has been offered yet Interesting DTs: – Vikings “Big Citrus” backup DT/NT small snaps. Rookie Rd3 Iowa St – Packers Chris McClellan rotational DT/1T. Rookie Rd3 Missouri – Giants Darius Alexander rotational 3/4i DL. 2025 Rd3 Toledo https://t.co/NU45yTIkL5 pic.twitter.com/2O2tmztQ00 — Jay Robins (@TheJayRobins) October 31, 2026 Domonique “Big Citrus” Orange is a shorter 6’1.875” but hulking near 330 lb Nose Tackle/ 1 Technique who would be a natural fit as a successor to Grover Stewart to help demand double teams in the interior and defend the run. One of the most beautiful plays from week 2 courtesy of Big Citrus pic.twitter.com/lNFC1C65AG — Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) August 23, 2026 Arguably one of the best run defenders of the 2026 NFL Draft, Orange could go a long way to helping fix the Colts run defense. Chris McClellan is a 6’3 and 317 lb defender who also can play the same position as Orange and is closer to Grover Stewart’s size (6’4 and 314 lb.). He previously played as a Defensive End in college before shifting inside and getting 6 sacks in his final year at Missouri. Plays with a lot of power in his hands and a quick burst off the line. Chris McClellan quietly played the best game of his career on Thursday night pic.twitter.com/Ur3vc90lEB — Eli Berkovits (@BookOfEli_NFL) October 31, 2026 Finally the Colts could also see a hometown return with former local Indiana high schooler Darius Alexander being part of a trade package. The former Arizona Cardinal was traded to the Giants mid-2025 and was a rookie of the week nominee afterwards with his flashes as a pass rusher. Unlike the prior two linemen, Alexander isn’t a space eater but rather a gap shooter from 3 Technique (sometimes 5 Technique Defensive End). He would be part of a rotation with Adebawore and could line up alongside the breakout Colts defensive tackle in certain rush packages on clear passing downs. This former Toledo Rocket could help solidify a strong rotation at a crucial interior spot. Darius Alexander run STOP pic.twitter.com/xJrjxDEXRu — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 12, 2026 Whether it is one of these three young Defensive Tackles, or another team is willing to pay the price for Jonathan Taylor, the Colts will only make a trade if they get an offer that blows them away. Otherwise, expect Jonathan Taylor to remain a Colt. The former Wisconsin Badger is under contract through the 2028 season, by which time the Colts will likely have a new young Quarterback via the 2027 or 2028 Draft to hopefully turn into a new franchise QB. They could keep Taylor for the length of his deal as he is still only 27, or trade him in the 2026 offseason instead of midseason and still get a nice return (presuming health, knock on wood). The #Colts would be thrilled to keep RB Jonathan Taylor in Indy. But of course, it’s a business, so they have to consider all possibilities. A *massive* offer would obviously change the calculations. — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) October 31, 2026 The Colts can trade him after the 2026 season too & get a large return (if JT is healthy, knock on wood) The urgency is on the teams trading for him, not on Colts trading him away Whether the Colts will be anything in 2 yrs depends on how they use their war chest of cap & picks https://t.co/SoFyZUDt60 — Jay Robins (@TheJayRobins) October 31, 2026 The ball is in the rest of the NFL’s court. Should any team wants 3 potential playoff pushes with one of the best pure runners in the NFL leading their backfield, then they’ll have to pony up before the trade deadline… before one of their fellow competitors does instead.

title: Jaguars vs. Colts: Staff roundtable and game picks for Week 8
summary: Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable! This week, we’re previewing the Jacksonville Jaguars’ second divisional matchup of the season. They look to extend their 11-game home win streak against the rebuilding Indianapolis Colts. Question 1: What’s your top question/concern about the Jaguars this week? Dillon Appleman: Can they stop playing down to their competition? […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 7: Brenton Strange #85 of the Jacksonville Jaguars runs the ball during the fourth quarter of an NFL 2025 game against the Indianapolis Colts at Everbank Stadium on December 7, 2025 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable! This week, we’re previewing the Jacksonville Jaguars’ second divisional matchup of the season. They look to extend their 11-game home win streak against the rebuilding Indianapolis Colts. Question 1: What’s your top question/concern about the Jaguars this week? Dillon Appleman : Can they stop playing down to their competition? In their last two games, the Jaguars have lost to the Texans and were eight seconds away from losing to the Eagles. Those two opponents have a combined record of 4-10 this season, so it’s fair to question if they have a problem with elevating their game when the competition is poor. The Colts fit that same mold as a team that has basically punted on the season already, so I would like to see a more focused Jaguars team as they look to take a stranglehold over the AFC South. Travis Holmes : The Jaguars have been one of the NFL’s top run-stopping defenses over the last two seasons. But as my college coach always tells me, you’re only as good as your last game played. Can Anthony Campanile’s unit rebound from the 114-yard rushing performance it surrendered against the Houston Texans before the bye week? One major strength-versus-strength matchup to watch is that the Jaguars rank second in the NFL in explosive rushing gains allowed, surrendering just 7 over the first six games, while the Colts’ offense ranks eighth with 23. Limiting Jonathan Taylor is the first test. Eliminating the game-changing runs is the second. Gus Logue : Can Jacksonville’s secondary survive without Antonio Johnson? He should be back soon from his ankle injury, but with No. 3 safety Caleb Ransaw on injured reserve, depth is a concern at the position. The good news is that the limping Colts probably aren’t equipped to do anything about it. But could another worrisome game from the secondary spark a trade for a veteran to help solidify the unit, the way that Jakobi Meyers did for the passing offense last season? Henry Zimmer : My top questions are simply about if the Jaguars are going to add any talent at the deadline. Trades within the AFC South are not happening, but can the Jags get better by adding a player late? Defensive line help comes to mind first, but does adding someone there benefit or hurt in the long run? Question 2: What’s the key to a Jaguars victory this week? Dillon : The key to a Jaguars victory is to simply keep Jonathan Taylor from wrecking the game. The Colts are just 3-6 all-time against the Jaguars with Taylor in the backfield, but all three wins have come when Taylor has gone for over 100 yards. He drives the success of that offense, so the key is to prevent a big day, which should be expected considering the Jaguars’ dominance against the run under Anthony Campanille. Travis : Establishing the run game seems to be the primary focus heading into this week’s matchup. The Colts rank 22nd in the league in opponent rushing yards allowed per game, and that was before Indianapolis decided to trade away interior game-wrecker DeForest Buckner to San Francisco. Considering the Indianapolis front seven’s struggles with missed tackles and Bhayshul Tuten’s propensity to force them, this seems like a match made in heaven, especially with a potentially rainy Sunday in Duval. Gus : Quarterback play in high-leverage situations. I think we could end up looking at the box score and saying, “See, 150 rushing yards for the Jaguars and 50 rushing yards for the Colts, that’s where the game was won/lost!” But really — as much as I do expect the Jaguars to have success on the ground and the Colts to struggle on the ground — Jacksonville will win because they have the better quarterback to move the chains. Henry : The key to victory this week is playing simple. This is a Colts team that is nuking itself into oblivion and should be a pushover. Don’t make this game complicated and win outright. No need for jet sweeps on the half-yard line to a backup tight end. Trevor Lawrence should be out of this game in the fourth quarter. Make it simple. Question 3: Who will be an X-factor for the Jaguars this week ? Dillon : I have a giant microscope over the Colts’ rookie left guard, Jalen Farmer, vs. the Jaguars’ interior defensive line. After the Colts traded away perennial Pro Bowler Quenton Nelson, the Colts will be starting Farmer, who has all of three offensive snaps this season. I’m looking for a big day for Arik Armstead and/or Ruke Orhorhoro on Sunday. Travis : My X-factor for this week is Jacksonville rookie left guard Emmanuel Pregnon, who will face off against Colts interior defensive linemen Grover Stewart and Adetomiwa Adebawore . Pregnon has shown major promise throughout 2026, with only a few bumps along the rookie road. Adebawore, who the Colts seem to be doubling down on moving forward following the DeForest Buckner trade, has significantly improved his hand placement and quickness in 2026. If there’s an area of concern for the Jacksonville offense, it’s more than likely going to come from Indianapolis’ interior defensive line. Gus : Chris Rodriguez Jr., who finished with 11 carries for 55 yards in Week 6 compared to 12 carries for 39 yards for Bhayshul Tuten. I certainly expect Tuten to operate as Jacksonville’s lead back moving forward, and even to have a very productive second half of the season, but don’t forget about Rodriguez. Liam Coen wants this backfield to be a 1-2 punch. I could see C-Rod having a solid 50-yard, 1-TD outing on Sunday. Henry : Against a downtrodden Colts team, can the Jags manufacture some catches for Brian Thomas Jr. to potentially bolster his trade status before the deadline? This would be a lovely conspiracy if the Jags targeted BTJ upwards of a dozen times to get him maybe over 100 yards on the day and then immediately look to trade him. Strike while the iron is hot! Final score prediction? Dillon : Jaguars 30, Colts 13 Travis : Jaguars 21, Colts 13 Gus : Jaguars 26, Colts 9 Henry : Jaguars 35, Colts 10 What are your Week 8 predictions, Jaguars fans? full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 18: Mansoor Delane #5 of the Kansas City Chiefs walks on the field during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers at Arrowhead Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane was a midweek downgrade in practice this week as he continues managing a preseason shoulder injury. Matt Derrick of Chiefs Digest expects the designation to be removed once Thomas arrives in Denver. Delane’s impending absence, however, was not the only news on Saturday for Kansas City’s secondary. title: Chiefs-Broncos: 5 things to watch in Week 8 matchup
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs (5-1) will take on the Denver Broncos (5-2) Sunday afternoon in a pivotal AFC West matchup in Denver. The game is set to kick off at 3:25 Arrowhead time and will be broadcast on CBS from Empower Field at Mile High. This will be the second meeting of the season between […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs (5-1) will take on the Denver Broncos (5-2) Sunday afternoon in a pivotal AFC West matchup in Denver. The game is set to kick off at 3:25 Arrowhead time and will be broadcast on CBS from Empower Field at Mile High. This will be the second meeting of the season between the two teams, with the Chiefs winning the season opener 31-10. Since then, the Broncos have lost only once and are coming off a 30-16 victory over the Arizona Cardinals . The Chiefs were undefeated until last Sunday night, when they lost to the Seattle Seahawks 20-3 in a lackluster showing. With the division in the balance, this October matchup will carry weight and could have a major impact on the season’s outcome. Here are five things to watch. 1. Attacking Bo Nix The Broncos have had to fight and claw their way to five wins, with only one victory coming by more than one possession this season. One reason for their issues has been their offense, which ranks 30th in the league in yards per game at 270, and quarterback Bo Nix has been the culprit. While he has kept his turnovers in check — only three interceptions — he has averaged just 5.8 yards per completion, which ranks 29th in the NFL, and his inability to hit downfield passes has stalled the Broncos’ offense. Nix played better against the Cardinals but still only completed 51% of his passes in the win. "Bo Nix is completing 41% against man coverage this year, which is the lowest number NGS has dating back to 2018." – Dave Helman. The Athletic Football Show. — HBTC (@hbtCHIEFS) October 30, 2026 Nix is 3-2 in his career against the Chiefs, but two of his wins have come without Patrick Mahomes starting on the other side. If Kansas City can limit what Nix can do downfield and contain him in the pocket, the defense could have a big day. 2. Harrison Butker It’s never a positive when the kicker makes the “Five Things to Watch” list in back-to-back weeks, but an awful performance last week has put him back in the spotlight this week. Butker went just one-for-three in the Chiefs’ loss and has fallen to a mere 68% field goal percentage this season. The poor performance and growing issues led to speculation after the game that the Chiefs could bring in another kicker. On Wednesday, the Chiefs announced they had signed former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad to challenge Butker. During his prime, Tucker was one of the league’s best, but he has been out of football since 2024 and has been the center of a highly publicized off-field scandal that led to a ten-game league suspension in 2025. ST Coordinator Dave Toub says Justin Tucker was on his 5th Tryout in KC and during the Tryout he was 30/30 on Kicks ranging from XPs to 60+ Butker went 10/10 with Tucker standing right next to him yesterday on FGs per Toub. — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) October 29, 2026 Bringing in another kicker was necessary, especially since Butker needs to know his job isn’t safe. Another poor performance could spell the end of the road for the Chiefs’ long-time kicker. Let’s hope this is the wake-up call Butker needs to turn his season around. 3. Third downs This week should feature some crucial third-down looks and will put both teams to the test. The Broncos have one of the league’s best third-down defenses, allowing only a 33% conversion rate, ranking second in the NFL. Their offense has been a different story, converting only 31% of their third-down attempts, which ranks second to last in the NFL. The Chiefs offense has been middle of the pack converting on third downs, currently ranked 15th with a 39% conversion rate. A poor showing on third downs in Seattle has dropped them down the rankings, and things won’t get any easier this week against the Broncos. Mahomes has a clean pocket here and wants to scramble right away, possibly to get the first down with his legs. Seattle was all over the mesh look and had LB's ready for Mahomes legs. Mahomes was hit from behind and was lucky to retain possession. pic.twitter.com/SlGnUmDcjK — Caleb James (@CJScoobs) October 27, 2026 On the other end, the Chiefs defense has been uncharacteristically bad on third down this year. They’ve allowed 43% on third-down conversions to opponents this season and were exploited by Seattle last week on third-and-long situations. The Chiefs offense will face another tough test on third down, while the defense can use this week to get sorted out. 4. Chiefs pass rush The Chiefs’ defensive line needs a much better week rushing the passer than last week. Against Seattle, the defense recorded zero sacks and just two quarterback hits. This season, the Chiefs rank 29th in sacks (8) and 26th in pressures (50), according to Pro Football Reference . The Chiefs’ defensive line has been lackluster, with no player recording more than a sack and only one player with double-digit quarterback hits on the season — George Karlaftis with 15. The Chiefs’ high-dollar players, Karlaftis and Chris Jones, have not produced up to their usual standard, with age possibly becoming a reality for the 32-year-old Jones as he prepares for his 162nd career game. Chiefs DC Steve Spagnuolo on DT Chris Jones: "Chris has been in the league a long time… We're going to rely on him to find a way to win. There are times that I think he's winning… Hopefully, it'll all come together for him… I want the same things you do. I want to rush… — Charles Goldman (@goldmctNFL) October 29, 2026 Felix Anudike-Uzomah and Ashton Gillotte have both made contributions, but neither has put together a steady string of pass rush. Rookie Peter Woods has also shown flash as a run defender, but he has yet to make a mark as a pass rusher. Fellow rookie R Mason Thomas has flashed week after week, but finished with only one sack — against Denver — despite impressive pressure in every game. This week, they will face the challenge of a mobile quarterback in Nix, who has been sacked only nine times this season — four times in Week 1 against Kansas City. The defense has been good this season, but the pass rush needs to step up to reach the next level. 5. Rashee Rice ’s return After one of the worst passing performances of the Mahomes-and-Reid era, the Chiefs will get an injection of talent at receiver as Rashee Rice returns after missing the last two weeks with a hamstring injury. Through four games, Rice has 190 yards on 13 receptions and one touchdown. He appeared to be building momentum with back-to-back 80+ yard games in Weeks 2 and 3, but didn’t record a catch in Week 4 when he injured his hamstring. His presence will be a welcome sight for Mahomes, and it will be worth watching how much the Chiefs try to distribute the ball to him. Mahomes had this to say about Rice during his press conference on Wednesday. “He’s such a physical receiver,” Mahomes shared. “He does a great job within the zone concepts and stuff like that, at getting himself open, as well as being physical versus man. And so having him back out there will be big for us because it’ll help take some pressure off the other guys to make plays and let them go out there and be themselves, and hopefully, we can have some success.”

title: Chiefs-Broncos: 5 questions with Mile High Report ahead of Week 8
summary: On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Denver Broncos in the late afternoon slot of Week 8 games. We welcome Ian St. Clair of Mile High Report — our sister SBNation site covering the Broncos— for Five Questions with the Enemy. Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Mile […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday, the Kansas City Chiefs face the Denver Broncos in the late afternoon slot of Week 8 games. We welcome Ian St. Clair of Mile High Report — our sister SBNation site covering the Broncos— for Five Questions with the Enemy . Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device and join the Mile High Report community through Sunday’s game to get perspectives from both sides of the Week 8 matchup! 1. The Broncos lost 31-10 in Kansas City to open the season but have since won five of six games, including three consecutive victories entering this rematch. What has changed the most about Denver since that Week 1 loss? The defense remembered how to tackle. In all seriousness, just put that horrible showing out of their minds and move on. However, getting humbled can also help level a person or team. The shellacking from the Chiefs was a great reminder that what happened last season has no bearing on the current one. So the Broncos better buckle up. And we’ve seen that in the last six games. The fact they’ve won five of six, with the gauntlet they had to start the season, is a testament to that. 2. Bo Nix produced two explosive touchdowns against Arizona, including a franchise-record 62-yard quarterback run, but he is still completing only 59.2% of his passes and averaging 182 passing yards per game. How would you evaluate Nix’s development through the first seven games? Nix has been bad to start this season. He’s had his moments: the second half against the Jacksonville Jaguars and Los Angeles Rams , the two drives against the Seattle Seahawks in the first half (way more than Patrick Mahomes did against that defense), and then Sunday against the Cardinals. But he’s looked and played like a shell of himself to start this season. However, Nix played similarly to this in his rookie season and last season, so he has had sluggish starts. We’ll see if his performance against Arizona is the confidence builder that gets him and the offense clicking. Of course, all of this is easier to swallow when Denver is 5-2. 3. Seattle held the Chiefs to three points and limited Kenneth Walker III to 36 rushing yards last week. Denver leads the NFL with 21 sacks and could face a Kansas City offensive line starting backup tackles. How much of Seattle’s defensive blueprint can the Broncos reproduce in this rematch? Honestly, just tackling Walker would be an improvement for the Broncos’ defense. But there’s no doubt defensive coordinator Vance Joseph and his assistants will look at what the Seahawks did and find ways to implement that in Sunday’s game plan. What will help Denver is the likely return of Patrick Surtain II, who has been out the last few games, and Jonathan Cooper, who missed the first game of the season. Something to keep an eye on, however, is Talanoa Hufanga has been ruled out , and now Brandon Jones showed up on the injury report with a hamstring. So potentially being down your starting safeties isn’t ideal. But Denver’s defense will be incredibly motivated on Sunday to replicate what Seattle did and make up for the Week 1 performance. 4. Jonah Coleman returned against Arizona and joined J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey in what has become a three-man backfield. Which Denver running back should the Chiefs consider the greatest threat entering Sunday’s game? Running the ball, it’s Coleman. He runs much better than Dobbins right now and is a more dangerous threat with the ball. Payton said after the Cardinals win that Coleman needs more touches, so Coleman should get them on Sunday. As a receiving threat, that’s Harvey, as he showed on the 52-yard touchdown reception. So KC should prepare for more running back screens this Sunday. 5. Kansas City enters the game at 5-1, with Denver right behind at 5-2, making this an important early battle for control of the AFC West and positioning within the AFC playoff race. How do you see Sunday’s rematch playing out, including your final score prediction and how much control the winner will gain in the division race? This is going to be a close game that will likely come down to the fourth quarter. Denver’s defense will play much better than that putrid showing to open the season. I also think Nix and the offense will build off last week against Arizona. The fact that the Broncos are playing at home gives them the edge, and they’ll get the 24-20 victory. That will put Denver in the lead for the AFC West, and with Kansas City’s upcoming schedule, puts it in a great spot to defend the division title.
author: Maurice Elston

full_text: (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs will take on the Denver Broncos on Sunday afternoon for the second time this season. In the first game, the Chiefs’ defense held Denver to just two third-down conversions over 12 attempts; Kansas City even stopped the Broncos’ only attempt at fourth down. The Chiefs haven’t been as stout on the crucial down since, including allowing the Seattle Seahawks to convert 11 of 16 third downs last week. Chiefs Kingdom, bring the noise to the SB Nation app! Join fellow Chiefs fans to react to every explosive play and game-changing moment in real time. Chat live throughout the game Browse with fewer ads Easily jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Download the SB Nation app on your mobile device! For Apple devices, click here . For Android devices, click here . The latest Kansas City Chiefs news Third downs and what else to watch when Chiefs meet the Broncos for second time | The Kansas City Star “We had them in 10 third-and-7 plus,” defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo said. “But we only one four of them. That’s not good.” Maybe Sunday’s road game against the Broncos provides a bounce-back opportunity. Denver ranks 31st in third-down conversions, at 31.1%. Defensive tackle Chris Jones said he’d add to the list of issues against the Seahawks. “You take third downs, and you take tackling,” Jones said. “That kind of makes up the game.” Why doesn’t rookie Cyrus Allen play more? Here’s the uphill climb he faces with Chiefs | The Athletic “He told me to get my eyes up, watching the coverage. ‘Look at the coverage,’” Allen told The Athletic on Thursday in the Chiefs’ locker room. “We had a play that we were running to where I gotta get the other guys open. So, just looking at the coverage and knowing what I got to do to help them guys.” It’s a perfect snapshot of what Allen must consider — and everything he has to think about — as he aims to become a bigger part of the Chiefs offense in his rookie season. Chiefs get Rashee Rice back from injury for Broncos game | ESPN In four games this season, Rice has produced 13 receptions on 16 targets for 190 yards and a touchdown. “He’s such a physical receiver,” Mahomes said Wednesday of Rice. “He does a great job within the zone concepts at getting himself open, as well as being physical versus man [coverage]. Having him back out there will be big for us because it’ll help take some pressure off the other guys to make plays and let them go out there and be themselves. Hopefully, we can have some success.” NFL Week 8 picks: Upset and score predictions, matchup breakdowns for every game | NFL.com Can Vance Joseph’s unit provide that kind of ground defense this Sunday? It’s a tall task, though Denver has shown some improvement against the run during its current three-game win streak, yielding a middle-of-the-pack figure of 4.2 yards per carry during that span. After spending the first six weeks of the season on the Commissioner’s Exempt List, Jonathon Cooper just made his season debut last Sunday, reinfusing the defense with a powerful edge setter. Meanwhile, the Chiefs’ offensive line is highly unstable beyond the Pro Bowl combo of C Creed Humphrey and RG Trey Smith. Here are 4 free agent WRs Kansas City Chiefs should consider signing | Chiefs Wire Darius Slayton A former New York Giant and Indianapolis Colt, Slayton is exactly the type of veteran presence who could immediately make an impact for the Chiefs’ offense as head coach Andy Reid makes mid-season adjustments to his legendary air attack. Curtis Samuel Samuel is a versatile threat who would have no problem earning touches in Kansas City’s offense as both a rusher and receiver. Around the NF L Panthers fire defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero, make other defensive changes after Packers loss | CBS Sports Evero’s unit struggled almost across the board in his four seasons running the Panthers defense. The lone bright spot was Carolina’s pass defense, where they allowed the fourth-fewest passing yards per game (201.1) since 2023. Evero wasn’t anywhere close to having his ideal secondary in the Thursday night loss at Lambeau Field. Cornerbacks Jaycee Horn (quad), Mike Jackson (groin) and Akayleb Evans (knee/triceps) were all on injured reserve in Week 8. Sean Payton goes for his 200th career win on Sunday | Pro Football Talk Payton’s next win will give him 200 for his career, including the postseason. His first crack at No. 200 comes on Sunday against the Chiefs. He has coached 319 games, generating a record of 199-120. He’s 189-110 in the regular season and 10-10 in the playoffs. With two more wins, Payton will catch Dan Reeves and Mike Tomlin for 10th on the all-time list. Four more wins after that will put Payton even with Marty Schottenheimer, at 205. Chuck Noll is No. 8 with 209. Paul Brown is No. 7 with 222. Records show 3 other women accused Packers’ Josh Jacobs of abuse after arrest | ESPN As police investigated whether to file charges against Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs following a May altercation with his then-girlfriend, multiple other women contacted police to detail their own allegations against him. Those accounts were included in evidence regarding Jacobs’ battery case that the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department released Friday night in response to a public records request. Green Bay TV station NBC 26 first reported the records release. Jacobs pleaded no contest Sept. 10 to misdemeanor counts of battery and criminal damage to property. He was arrested May 26, three days after an incident in which a woman said he threw her to the ground. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Kingdom Keys: 3 Keys to a Chiefs victory over the Broncos in Week 8 Kansas City’s defensive ends must remain disciplined. George Karlaftis and the other edge defenders cannot consistently rush beyond Nix and create open escape lanes. Collapsing the pocket means little if Nix can step outside it and turn a broken play into a first down. The Chiefs should make him beat them by consistently throwing from inside the pocket. Nix has completed 59.2% of his passes while averaging only 5.8 yards per attempt, with seven touchdowns, three interceptions and an 80.7 passer rating.
