summary: The Los Angeles Chargers are facing off against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 8 at SoFi Stadium fresh off the bye. The Chargers have lost their first six games and are the only winless team left in the league. However, the Chargers can turn things around with a win against the crosstown rival Rams. […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - AUGUST 27: Los Angeles Rams tight end Mark Redman (83) catches the ball for a gain during the NFL preseason game between the Los Angeles Chargers and the Los Angeles Rams on August 27, 2026 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers are facing off against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 8 at SoFi Stadium fresh off the bye. The Chargers have lost their first six games and are the only winless team left in the league. However, the Chargers can turn things around with a win against the crosstown rival Rams. Per FanDuel Sportsbook , the Chargers are an underdog by 6.5 points. Let’s take a look at some predictions for the game. Over/Under: 45.5 Only one game the Chargers have played this season has had more than 45.5 points. That came against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 4. The Chargers’ offense has not been up to par, scoring 17 points or fewer in all but one game this year. The Rams should have a boost from the crowd, which will be unfortunate to deal with while the Chargers are also at their home stadium, but it’s hard to imagine the Los Angeles “bowl” as a barnburner. Prediction: Under Chargers +6.5 Fanduel is giving the Chargers a touchdown to work with, and they are coming off a bye week when they were able to get some much-needed rest. The Rams are coming into this game knowing they need to keep their foot on the gas after their blowout win against the Las Vegas Raiders last week, when they won 35-21. This win will put the Rams at 5-0 if they can get to it. I’m expecting a focused Rams team against the Chargers, which will likely result in a multi-score victory for the Rams. Prediction: Rams -6.5 Final Score It wouldn’t surprise me if the Chargers came out of the gates with a score or two, but given how they have performed throughout the season, it’s hard to imagine that this is the week they break their spell of bad luck. title: Two kickers are better than one?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams may be using two kickers and punter for their Week 8 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers. So, are the Rams then using three kickers? Seems that way. The Rams will go with Brandon McManus, Joshua Karty and then Ethan Evans as the punter. McManus will likely get the nod for […]
full_text: Football: Los Angeles Rams Josh Karty (16) warms up prior to game vs Baltimore Ravens at M&T StadiumBaltimore, MD 10/12/2025CREDIT: Simon Bruty (Photo by Simon Bruty/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images/Getty Images) (Set Number: X164783) The Los Angeles Rams may be using two kickers and punter for their Week 8 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers. So, are the Rams then using three kickers? Seems that way. The Rams will go with Brandon McManus, Joshua Karty and then Ethan Evans as the punter. McManus will likely get the nod for field goals while Karty is maybe possibly expected to handle kickoffs. It’s interesting as the Rams truly are trying anything they can to get the special teams improved. Will it work? If not, truly what else will the Rams be able to try? Sunday is a big test for the Rams and their much-maligned special teams unit. Sunday is a big test for the Rams in general. Rams will have 2 kickers vs. Chargers after promoting Joshua Karty (ramswire) “The Rams have used their activations for special teams in the past, usually for players who operate on the coverage/return teams. This time, the franchise is calling up kicker Joshua Karty and long snapper Jake McQuaide for the contest. Both players were on the team last season before being added to the practice squad this week. Karty, who was waived after missing multiple field goals and extra-point attempts, has a “knuckleball” kickoff that some in the media have pointed to as a potential solution for the team’s coverage issues. The Rams still have Brandon McManus on their roster, so it’s not clear what Karty’s role will be.“ Sean McVay’s crazy two-kicker gamble might actually be genius (sports.yahoo) “Even last Sunday against Las Vegas, McManus watched Raiders returners rip off gains of 42 and 39 yards. McVay eventually resorted to asking him to kick the ball through the end zone. That’s not fixing the problem. That’s surrendering to it. Enter Karty back through the door he first entered when he was drafted by the Rams in the sixth round of the 2024 NFL Draft. The former Rams kicker developed a knuckleball-style kickoff that resembles a soccer free kick, deliberately striking the football with minimal spin to create unpredictable movement.“ Is Puka Nacua Playing Today? (Injury Update, Betting Impact for Chargers vs. Rams in NFL Week 8) (si.com) “Still, with the Rams down Davante Adams (hamstring), the L.A. offense is going to run through Nacua as long as he can be out on the field. The star wideout still played in 84.7 percent of the team’s offensive snaps in Week 7, catching eight of his 10 targets for 68 yards and a score. This season, Nacua has 45 catches on 62 targets for 485 yards and two scores in just five games. He’s averaging over 12 targets per game, which gives him an extremely high floor when it comes to the prop market.“ 3 Rams veterans who likely won’t be back next season (ramblinfan) “General manager Les Snead faces a difficult challenge in managing the current roster while setting up the same team to succeed next season. The Rams have more than two dozen pending free agents, many of whom are at risk of not returning. Extension dollars will be limited. Here are three veterans whose return is unlikely. Rams may have already decided to part ways with these 3 veterans 1. Wide receiver Tutu Atwell The trade that reunited the Rams with Atwell made little sense when it was announced . It makes even less sense now. Despite limited snaps from Puka Nacua and Davante Adams, and a lack of production from the remaining receivers, Atwell sits on the bench. That’s even more confusing when tight end injuries are factored in.“ 3 major storylines ahead of Rams vs. Chargers (sports.yahoo) “The season is young, but wins in the NFL are scarce. The Green Bay Packers are currently holding down the last wild-card spot after their Thursday night win against the Carolina Panthers , and the Rams host them on Thanksgiving Eve. Just saying. For the Chargers, it’s even worse. With the trade deadline looming, players and coaches are competing for their livelihoods. Desperation drives the narrative. Sunday special team scaries The Rams’ special teams have been a letdown this whole season, and their kick coverage team has been simply awful. Now, the team has brought back kicker Joshua Karty and long-snapper Jake McQuaide on their practice squad, activating them both for this game.“ Rams vs. Chargers Prediction, Odds, Pick For NFL Week 8 (foxsports) “The Rams lead the NFL in total offense (399.1 yards per game) and are coming off a season-high 35 points against the Raiders. Matthew Stafford has thrown eight touchdowns against one interception over his last three games, completing 75.9% of his passes with a 113.4 passer rating. The Chargers are the NFL’s last winless team at 0-6 and lead the league with 15 giveaways.“ Rams defense ready for challenges Justin Herbert presents (ramswire) “Despite the lack of overall offensive success, Herbert has displayed enough, paired with his defense, to keep games close, prompting the Rams’ defense to focus on stopping him. Defensive coordinator Chris Shula detailed the challenges Herbert presents. “I see that he’s tall, strong, stands tall in the pocket, tough,” said Shula. He sees the whole field, can activate the whole field. A bunch of playmakers, guys running, disperses it, gets the guys out. You see a really good player. Obviously, I know they’re not exactly where they want to be right now, but you see everything is out there for him to be a great offense.” Can the Rams replicate a balanced offense against the Chargers? (ocregister) “The offense as a whole fed off their energy, too, with receivers suddenly finding more room to operate as defenses had to respect the run on play-action calls. “Being able to get these [defensive backs] to take that extra yard or two up to bite on the run fake and it allows us to play with more grass. The more grass that we have to play with, the more confident No. 9 is in being able to let that one go,” receiver Puka Nacua said. “The confidence that he has in letting the ball go is always at 100 percent, but I think when there’s more grass, it goes past 100.” Head coach Sean McVay sometimes bristles when asked about “balanced” play calling. He doesn’t want to be locked into running 50% run plays and 50% pass plays just because of the concept of balance.“ Ian Rapoport’s Myles Garrett injury update brings ‘optimism’ (clutchpoints) ““There is optimism that Myles Garrett returns to practice this week. I know there was optimism last week, and much more this week. He should practice and should be on the field playing relatively quickly,” Rapoport wrote on X, formerly Twitter.“ Rams, Chargers on collision course with same problems, on and off the field (usatoday) “The Los Angeles Chargers are a woeful 0-6 . The Los Angeles Rams are a disappointing 3-4 . And as the teams head into their game Sunday, Nov. 1 at SoFi Stadium, they’re struggling with another problem. Both teams are struggling off the field as measured by their fan bases. The Nielsen Scarborough NFL Fandom Index released in August highlights the issue. Only one in four adults in the Los Angeles market watched, streamed, attended, listened to or followed the Rams in the past year, based on data available when the study was released. That accounted for 24% of the Los Angeles market and left roughly 11 million adults with no connection to the Rams.“ Comment of the day: Feed post of the day:

title: Rams should have drafted at least 1 rookie who could help
summary: The Los Angeles Rams are getting nothing from their rookie class, and they’re paying the price for it midway through the season, as their five draft picks have played a combined six games, four of which are Max Klare, who has played one offensive snap all year. It’s not entirely the players’ fault, of course […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams are getting nothing from their rookie class, and they’re paying the price for it midway through the season, as their five draft picks have played a combined six games, four of which are Max Klare, who has played one offensive snap all year. It’s not entirely the players’ fault, of course — injuries and other factors are playing into this, too — and it’s not like the Rams had a ton of picks to flood the zone with young contributors, either. But in a season that’s been complicated and difficult for myriad reasons, not having any young potential contributors to bank on has been just another challenge for Sean McVay and company. Where it Started This issue begins with the 13th overall pick, quarterback Ty Simpson. That selection has been debated over and over , but whether or not it pans out doesn’t change the fact that Los Angeles eschewed taking a potential immediate contributor for a gamble on the future. He hasn’t taken a single snap this season and isn’t likely to, but if Les Snead is going to draft a third-string quarterback that early, shouldn’t he have also considered landing immediate contributors later? The rest of the rookie class has combined to play six games this year and one — defensive tackle Tim Keenan — isn’t even on the team anymore. In fact, Keenan has played 19 snaps on the Raiders this season. That’s 15 more snaps than the rest of L.A.‘s 2026 rookie class combined on offense or defense — and he did it against the Rams! We have elevated DT Tim Keenan and DE Cian Slone from the practice squad. pic.twitter.com/5pDkXjEvRW — Las Vegas Raiders (@Raiders) October 24, 2026 This offseason, Los Angeles steered all the way into the multiple-tight end trend it was on the cutting edge of in 2025, including taking Max Klare out of Ohio State in the second round. He’s currently buried on the depth chart and has played exactly one offensive snap in four games, with 12 more on special teams. If the Rams wanted a tight end, should they have drafted Kenyon Sadiq in the first round and then explored quarterback options later? Obviously Snead had quite the affinity for Simpson, but L.A. still seemed to value him quite a bit higher than other teams. We’re also not close to a place, yet, to declare that Simpson will be a better quarterback than third-rounders Carson Beck and Drew Allar. Snead may have even been able to trade up from the second-round for Simpson, a move we know the GM likes quite a bit, as he did something similar for Braden Fiske in 2024. The Rams have Davis Allen out there scoring touchdowns after burning a 2nd round draft pick so that Max Klare can be their TE5.. pic.twitter.com/cz2W8Zda2v — Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT (@jmthrivept) October 25, 2026 Wide receiver C.J. Daniels, meanwhile, played three offensive snaps without a target against the Las Vegas Raiders, and that’s it for his production. As you may or may not have noticed, the Rams could use some help at wide receiver right now. Offensive lineman Keagen Trost, a third-round pick, has unfortunately been behind the 8 ball this year due to injuries. He was activated from injured reserve earlier this month but still hasn’t debuted. Rookie Help, When? Banking on draft picks to save a season is, historically, not an especially fruitful endeavor. In fairness to Los Angeles, the plan for the draft this year was to build for the future instead of finding quick fixes, considering it had the best roster in the NFL on paper in the spring (and well into the summer and fall). The reasonable assumption is that this front office found players they identified as pieces they could develop that would eventually be useful contributors once some of the older stars were phased out. But teams have consistently found rookie contributors that help them win Super Bowls, even when those teams are loaded: The Seahawks had Nick Emmanwori and Grey Zabel last year The Eagles had Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean in 2025 The Chiefs had Rashee Rice in 2024 Football, like life, doesn’t always go according to plan. If the Rams have the best front office in the NFL, then they shouldn’t be afraid to give meaningful snaps to rookies, as their rivals do it every year with much success. And it’s not like “wait until next year” always works for the Rams. This year was “next year” for Terrance Ferguson and Josaiah Stewart and Jarquez Hunter, who is no longer on the team. It’s still too early to panic, especially fresh off a dominant win a week ago, but it certainly would be nice for the Rams to be getting something at all from their rookies. At this stage of the game, though, any contributions from that small group will likely be either a bonus or pure desperation.

title: Rams vs Chargers: How to watch on TV, stream, or listen on radio

full_text: Looking for their first back-to-back wins of 2026, the 3-4 Los Angeles Rams take on the winless Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday November 1. FOX is set to televise the 1:o5 p.m. PDT kickoff from SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Ca. With the two organizations sharing the same stadium, it is the Rams that have been designated as the home team. 2026 has been a struggle for the o-6 Chargers, but coming in to the game off a bye week, they should be refreshed, healed up, and ready for a clean slate. The Bolts have struggled on offense, rating in the Bottom 3 of the NFL in total points scored (90), total yards (1723), yards per play (4.6), passing yards (1009), percentage of drives ending in a score (25.4), and have the highest percentage of drives ending in a turnover (19.7). On the other hand, the Rams are towards the top of NFL stats in both offense and defense. Allowing opponents (mostly lesser) to hang around too long, self-inflicted wounds, and horrendous special teams play has them needing this win to get back to .500 and stay within reach of the six teams that are ahead or tied with them in the wild card race. The injury bug has really embedded under the Rams skin and Week 8 is no different. L.A. has four starters with a questionable designation, center Coleman Shelton (hip). tight end Colby Parkinson (ribs), wide receiver Jordan Whittington (back), and cornerback Trent McDuffie (groin). Long snapper Joe Cardona is doubtful with a bad ankle. Here’s how to follow the game! Location: SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Ca, Date: Sunday, November 1 Time: 1:05 p.m. PDT Watch on TV Nationally: FOX Play-By-Play: Adam Amin Color Analyst: Drew Brees Sideline Reporter: Kristina Pink Streaming In past seasons, a live stream was available on the following platforms if the game is available on TV in the local market. title: Rams may have new longsnapper for Week 8
summary: The Los Angeles Rams are still trying to figure out their special teams. They will continue to keep trying. It’s a work in progress. full_text: The Los Angeles Rams are still trying to figure out their special teams. They will continue to keep trying. It’s a work in progress. Rams’ special teams unit gets more bad news with long snapper doubtful (ramswire) “Cardona did not practice on Wednesday or Thursday. If McQuaide does play, he will be the sixth specialist to take a snap for Los Angeles this season, joining Cardona, Ethan Evans, Harrison Mevis, Blake Grupe, and Brandon McManus. McQuaide was the Rams’ long-snapper to end the 2025 season, replacing Alex Ward. He was excellent, helping the team reach the NFC Championship Game. He also played for the Rams from 2011 to 2020, earning Pro Bowl honors in 2016 and 2017. McQuaide also played for the Dallas Cowboys, Detroit Lions , Chicago Bears , Minnesota Vikings , Miami Dolphins , and Pittsburgh Steelers, either as a member of the active roster or the practice squad.“ Joshua Karty and Jake McQuaide add former Rams experience to current Rams special teams (rams.com) “McVay was asked on Wednesday if Karty would be utilized on kickoffs, to which McVay said he would “work through those things and kind of just see how the week goes.” On Friday, McVay said Karty being activated to the 48-man gameday roster would be contingent on some of the other injuries throughout the roster that have occurred throughout the week. McVay also said he thinks Karty’s ability to potentially impact kickoffs would impact that decision. The Rams decided to replace Karty with Mevis after Week 9 of last season. Karty’s production dropped from 85.3% on field goals his rookie season to 66.7% in his second season through eight games. Karty said on Wednesday that during training camp last year he was “dealing with a little hip thing” and “probably should have just rested for a bit in fall camp.” Experts overwhelmingly favor Rams over winless Chargers in Week 8 (sports.yahoo) “Of the 52 picks across USA Today, Bleacher Report, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, CBS Sports, The Athletic and NFL.com, 47 have the Rams winning. The only five picking the Chargers are all from Bleacher Report. The Rams are coming off a 35-21 win over the Raiders in Week 7, which snapped a two-game losing streak after back-to-back defeats to the Bills and Cardinals . Kyren Williams and Blake Corum combined for 192 rushing yards and two touchdowns in Week 7, and Matthew Stafford threw three touchdown passes. A win Sunday would give Los Angeles back-to-back victories for the first time this season and set them up nicely for the second half of the year.“ Rams are ‘fixing’ special teams like a bad mechanic repairs a car (ramblinfan) “If you take an automobile for repairs to a bad mechanic, the telltale sign is the incessant swapping of parts that merely runs up the tab without fixing the problem. A dependable mechanic determines the problem and effects the necessary repairs. The difference is felt in the time at the shop and a much less expensive repair bill. Nobody is pointing the finger at general manager Les Snead – he’s doing what he can with a defective motor – but right now LA is merely swapping parts without a clue . Rams still grasping at straws to fix woeful special teams The entire ‘let’s see who can play?’ facade is something fans expected to be settled during training camp or, at worst, preseason. The issue is still at a tipping point approaching midseason. That’s not a good situation for a team that has struggled to stay at .500, while clinging to playoff aspirations.“ Hypothetical Rams trade sends mid-round picks for WR (ramswire) “In a hypothetical trade proposal, Nguyen has Los Angeles sending a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to Jacksonville for Thomas. He argues the Rams made a mistake in the draft by not upgrading the offense that this deal could fix. The Rams tried to play it too cute in the draft and live in two timelines, taking quarterback Ty Simpson with the 13th pick when the best option this season would have been a receiver. Davante Adams is 33 and had hamstring issues last season — it wasn’t hard to predict he would miss games this season. Puka Nacua has had injury and off-field issues. How would KC Concepcion — whom I rated higher than Makai Lemon — look in their offense? They could rectify that mistake by trading for Thomas Jr. The Jaguars should be much more willing to trade Thomas Jr. to the NFC, rather than an AFC contender. Thomas Jr. would infuse much-needed speed to the offense, while his vertical route tree would complement Nacua, who makes his living in the middle of the field.“ Los Angeles Rams vs. Los Angeles Chargers Fantasy Football Matchup Breakdown For Week 8 (fantasylife) “ No way I was the only one circling this game on the schedule before the season even kicked off, thinking we’d be previewing a potential Super Bowl matchup. Can’t even tell you how many Justin Herbert MVP tickets I saw posted on socials this summer. Well, that ain’t happening — we’re seven weeks in, and these two LA teams combined for one total win in the entire month of October. Oof. “ Matthew Stafford Gets Concerning Update Before Rams Game (heavy.com) “Whittington is not a significant part of the Rams’ passing game. He has just two receptions for 12 yards on the season, and a 42-476-0 line for his career so far, which began as a sixth-round pick (213th overall) of the 2024 draft. However, while not one of Stafford’s top targets, he is a strong blocker on the perimeter. The Rams are already without Davante Adams (hamstring, IR) and Puka Nacua admitted this week that he is still managing the calf injury that popped up in practice last week.“ Rams Hit With Concerning Injury News Before Facing Chargers (sports.yahoo) “At this point in time, no one knows exactly when Garrett will return. There was hope that the Rams could open up his practice window this week, but that didn’t end up being the case . The current hope is that Adams could return in the shorter window of the original 6-to-8 week estimate. Going up against the Chargers should give L.A. a good chance to pick up another win. Jim Harbaugh and his team are 0-6 and not many positive signs of improvement have been seen. Hopefully, some of these updates receive good news before Sunday afternoon’s game. Kickoff this week against the Chargers is scheduled for 4:05 p.m. ET. Fans will be able to tune in and watch the game on Fox.“ Rams face injury concerns ahead of Chargers game as McVay praises defense, Aaron Donald (sportingtribune) “”Dylan McMahon has done a great job this week,” McVay said. “He’s had a lot of work. Ryan Wendell is always really good about getting a good rotation of guys, especially at that center position. Dylan’s had a lot of work this week because of the approach we’ve taken with Coleman. I think he’s handled it really well.” Whittington’s status could also affect the Rams’ special teams plans, including whether kicker Joshua Karty is elevated for the game. McVay said the staff has to consider how losing Whittington would affect the 48-player game-day roster and the team’s ability to handle injuries during the game. The Rams are already without two offensive playmakers: wide receiver Davante Adams and tight end Terrance Ferguson.“ PODCAST: Chargers Football Therapy: Can Justin Herbert Spark a Reset Against the Rams? (sports.yahoo) “At the Playbook Restaurant, the discussion turns to simplifying responsibilities without becoming predictable. Can the Chargers build a smaller, more dependable collection of concepts that allows players to operate confidently? There is room to laugh, too. Reasonable Request or Chargers Fan Delusion separates realistic expectations from emotional wish lists, while the Chargers Emotional Support Draft asks which improvement would matter most: protection, rushing production, red-zone finishing or cleaner execution. Plus, get a Rams matchup framework, an appreciation for overlooked contributions and a schedule look ahead featuring Houston, Baltimore, the Jets and New England. Expect…

title: Raiders should take initiative and blitz Jets offense often in Week 8
summary: Geno Smith gets rattled when blitzed. That’s not some grand revelation on the veteran quarterback. It’s the plain truth and Raider Nation is all too aware of this. Smith was the Las Vegas Raiders starting quarterback last season for then-head coach Pete Carroll and the West Virginia product was like a lamb to slaughter that […]
full_text: (Heidi Fang/Las Vegas Review-Journal/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Geno Smith gets rattled when blitzed. That’s not some grand revelation on the veteran quarterback. It’s the plain truth and Raider Nation is all too aware of this. Smith was the Las Vegas Raiders starting quarterback last season for then-head coach Pete Carroll and the West Virginia product was like a lamb to slaughter that year. Due to a porous offensive line — due in large part to both talent and coaching — Smith was sacked a league-high 55 times while throwing 19 touchdowns and an NFL-leading 17 interceptions as a 15-game starter. Smith is enjoying a rebound season in his return to the New York Jets — the team that drafted him 39th overall in the 2013 NFL Draft — as he’s completing 70 percent of his passes with 10 touchdowns, two interceptions, and 1,623 passing yards. Smith is keeping Gang Green in games and still continues to throw a nice deep ball. But when opponents dial up the pressure and send extra defenders beyond the standard four-man rushes, Smith continues to wilt. Behind New York’s offensive line, Smith has been sacked 21 times which is fourth-most behind the Cleveland Browns’ Deshaun Watson (25), the Carolina Panthers’ Bryce Young (23), and the Pittsburgh Steelers’ Aaron Rodgers (22). Conventional wisdom says Las Vegas doesn’t need to blitz to create pressures. According to Pro Football Reference (PFR), Rob Leonard’s Raiders defense ranks fifth with 73 total pressures and is third in pressure percentage at 29.2 percent . That’s percentage only behind the league-leading (and domineering) Minnesota Vikings at 35.7 percent and the Seattle Seahawks at 30.9 percent. The 2026 Bengals defense plays exactly the way you would want to against the Ravens The Bengals blitz at the league's lowest rate (17.8%) but still generate pressure at a top-5 rate (39.3%). Over the last two years, the Ravens rank 3rd-best in EPA per dropback when blitzed… pic.twitter.com/8g4mF6n1wz — Scott Barrett (@ScottBarrettDFB) October 23, 2026 Coincidentally, the defensive play callers for both the Vikings (Brian Flores) and Seahawks (Mike Macdonald) are coaches Leonard learned from during his career enroute to getting elevated to defensive coordinator by Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak. Seattle paces the league with 77 total pressures with the Denver Broncos (76), Vikings (74) and Atlanta Falcons (74) ahead of Las Vegas in that regard — for comparison. But to truly shake Smith’s confidence and ground the Jets air attack, blitzing is a solid course of action to create chaos. Blitzing shouldn’t be relegated to just quell the pass but stonewall the run, too. Leonard’s defense got gashed badly in Las Vegas’ four-straight losses giving up 656 total rushing yards total in those games . The 199 yards yielded to the Los Angeles Rams’ ground game in Week 7 being the highest tally so far this season. And the Raiders have given up 30 or more points in the last four games with a total of 143 points allowed in that span. No other team approaches that sum as the closest team to allow that amount: The Arizona Cardinals at 127 points. Blitzing the run can help mitigate the loose rush defense the Raiders exhibit. Offensive coordinator Frank Reich is orchestrating a Jets offense that’s 27th in points scored (137) and 23rd in yards gained (2,121). New York’s passing attack is ranked 21st in yards gained (1,445) and 19th in touchdowns (10) while the ground game is 22nd in yards (675) and 26th in touchdowns (four). If there’s an opponent to deploy blitzes upon, it’s the Jets. So far this season, PFR charts the Raiders defense with 61 blitzes (which is tied for 16th most among the 32 NFL teams with the Seahawks) for a 24.4 percentage on 1,611 passing attempts. The Vikings boast the most blitzes by far as Flores dialed up 140 so far (league-leading 67.6 percent of passing attempts). The Broncos are second with 95 and the New England Patriots are third at 92. (Interestingly enough, the Jets are tied for fourth most blitzes dialed up by head coach and defensive play caller Aaron Glenn). Just moments after the broadcast highlighted @nyjets QB Geno Smith not seeing a wide open receiver for what would have been an easy TD, he threads the needle on a deep ball to Omar Cooper. pic.twitter.com/ZmlwEJMj9a — Glenn Naughton (@JNRadio_Glenn) October 25, 2026 The trio of defenders Leonard’s activated on a blitz are: Linebackers Quay Walker (29) and Nakobe Dean (20) and slot cornerback Taron Johnson (13). Walker and Dean have four pressures apiece and two and 1.5 sacks, respectively. Johnson has our pressures, in comparison. Leonard also dials up the rush from safety Jeremy Chinn (five blitzes with a pressure and sack) and outside cornerback Eric Stokes (four blitzes, two pressures, one sack), and rookie safety Treydan Stukes (three blitzes). Disguising and selectively sending extra defenders at the Jets offensive line is an opportunity to both stop the run and attack the passing game. And at 3-4 overall and fourth-worst defense in terms of points allowed (197) and yards given up (2,616) the Raiders should go for broke and dial up the pressure to help a young secondary and give sack leaders Kwity Paye and Malcolm Koonce (three sacks, apiece) and Maxx Crosby (two) much-needed reinforcements. Leonard expects a fundamentally sound effort against New York this Sunday and in order to create the pass rush opportunities, need to be much more effective and stymie Gang Green’s ground game. Las Vegas has the eighth most missed tackles at 41, according to PFR. The Broncos pace the NFL with 56 whiffs, for comparison. “In the offense, you always hear them say they want a hat for a hat in the run game. One-on-one, they want to account for everybody and typically leave the corners unblocked. The expectation one-on-one is to win,” Leonard said during his media session this past Thursday. “So, it’s block release, pad level, hand placement and, like you said, whooping the guy in front of you. To me, we try to train the process of doing that. We obviously have got to do a better job. When you play like that, that starts with me. “When you have mis-fits, missed tackles and different angles to the ball, that is 100 percent on me. I have to be better there.” Asked Kwitty Paye how stopping the run could help the guys off the edge “stop the run, have some fun” #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/adGxbx3fyC — Alexa Belcastro (@alexabelcastro2) October 30, 2026 Quotes of Note “I told the defense yesterday I’m looking at it for everybody. There are very few, ‘Hey, Nakobe (Dean) is the starting Mike (middle linebacker). 98 (Maxx Crosby) is a defensive end.’ Everybody is competing for the job, myself included, every day. I want them to feel that because it’s true. There’s nothing guaranteed. I tell them, you have to put someone in a position to say, ‘How can I not play this guy? He does everything right.’ And until that happens with everybody, then competition’s on every day.” —Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard when asked about the competition between cornerback Darien Porter and Hezekiah Masses “We’re always scouting ourselves after games, looking at a one-game sample or a seven-game sample, and then just being honest with what we are doing well, how we can build on that, what we aren’t doing well, and the whys behind it, and then we take those things and try to formulate a plan to be ready for the next opponent.” —Las Vegas Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko when asked how the coaching staff determines where major adjustments need to be made

title: Raiders Mailbag: Should Las Vegas sell Maxx Crosby, Kolton Miller, other players ahead of NFL trade deadline?
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders have a chance to end their four-game losing streak against the New York Jets in Week 8. But we’re also less than two weeks away from the NFL Trade Deadline (Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 1:00 p.m. PST), which is the primary focus of this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! Q: […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders have a chance to end their four-game losing streak against the New York Jets in Week 8 . But we’re also less than two weeks away from the NFL Trade Deadline (Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 1:00 p.m. PST), which is the primary focus of this week’s mailbag. Let’s get to it! Q: Would be interesting to hear your take on trading Maxx Crosby, Jackson Powers-Johnson, Kolton Miller, Isaiah Palo-Mao and Kirk Cousins? Seems like the right thing to do given the team’s realistic timeline. A: I’ll start with the elephant in the room. I was a strong proponent of trading Crosby in the offseason and still think it would be in the Raiders’ best long-term interests to get multiple high-end draft picks for the 29-year-old. I think two first-rounders is probably out of the question now, but it doesn’t hurt that Jeffery Simmons — who is the same age and was in the same draft class as Crosby — just got dealt for two firsts and a fourth, with a fifth going back to Chicago. Also, Simmons is only under contract for one more year than Crosby is. So, I think John Spytek could get at least a comparable return for the edge rusher, and I don’t know how Spytek could say ‘no’ to an offer like that after the team’s playoff hopes came crumbling down this month. It doesn’t seem like Crosby is going anywhere, though, with Adam Schefter saying on Monday that “he means so much to that franchise” while pouring cold water on the trade talk/rumors. But if I’m calling the shots, I’m pulling the trigger if I can get at least a first- and a second-round pick for Crosby. I touched on this last week ; it feels like Powers-Johnson’s days in Las Vegas are numbered after getting benched. I don’t know if that happens ahead of the trade deadline, but barring a material change, I think JPJ will be shopped in the offseason. I liken it to Tyree Wilson from this past offseason, where a fresh start might be best for both sides, and don’t expect much more than a fifth-rounder in return. I’m all the way out on trading Miller ahead of the deadline. I know he has regressed, but if the plan is to have Fernando Mendoza play at any point this year, I’m not trusting Charles Grant to protect Mendoza’s blindside. Grant has barely seen the field, and at least the coaching staff knows what it can get from Miller, who has been a good pass protector in the past and is still solid right now. Could Grant be the long-term solution at left tackle? Sure, but turning the reins over to him now would be a massive risk, especially with a rookie quarterback/the future of the franchise. In the offseason, I could be convinced that it’s worth it to trade Miller because then the coaching staff has several months to get Grant ready and can bring in a veteran insurance policy in free agency. But midseason, trading Miller would be a bad idea, in my opinion. If there’s an offer, Pola-Mao would be easy to part with since he’s just a backup and special teamer right now. I just don’t know if there’s much of a market for that, barring an injury over the next two weekends. If IPM gets dealt, don’t expect much more than a sixth- for seventh-round pick swap or just a seventh-rounder. Also, he’s an impending free agent, so I could see Pola-Mao getting waived after the deadline to make room for Dalton Johnson on the game-day active roster. I feel like I’m in the minority on this, but I would rather see the Raiders hold onto Cousins even if Mendoza is playing. Trust me, as a draft freak, I love the idea of getting more picks. However, I think it reduces part of the rationale for having Cousins be Mendoza’s mentor if the former gets shipped away when the latter takes over. I know that has to happen at some point, but I think it’s valuable for the rookie to have a peer as a sounding board when things go wrong during his first handful of starts. Especially since Cousins has seen it all in the NFL, and those two have been forming a big brother-little brother type of relationship over the last six months. A: Well, as someone who watches and breaks down the Raiders’ defense every week, the past month was already pretty unwatchable, LOL! But to your point, if Crosby does get traded, that creates a need for an edge and adds to the already rather long list of needs. That’s why I wouldn’t make that trade for just one first-round pick, and the return would have to include multiple Top 100 selections. The plan for a Crosby-less defense in Vegas would hinge on Keyron Crawford bouncing back from injury and at least proving to be a quality second edge defender since Malcolm Koonce is on a one-year contract and Kwity Paye is trending toward being a bust/role player. Then, that’s where the two picks come in because one can be used to find Crosby’s replacement or the second edge if Crawford fills that role, and the second pick fills a different need like defensive tackle. Obviously, there are a lot of variables that can go wrong in there. But the defense has given up over 35 points per game over the last four weeks with Crosby on it. Several positions need to be addressed in the offseason, and he’ll be 30 in August. So, would you rather have a very good but aging player, or two chances to improve the team for the long haul? It’s a matter of preference, and there’s a good amount of risk involved in either scenario. But, again, I’d take my chances if the right offer comes across the desk. Q: Is it time to have a realistic discussion on Spytek? A: I got a lot of questions about Spytek this week, with several people asking if (or outright saying) he should get fired. I get it, the Raiders need to get a lot more return on their offseason investments. There’s no denying that, and Spytek’s Day 2 picks have produced little to nothing. Darien Porter is the best one so far, and Porter hasn’t been able to hold down a starting spot. But part of the reason why the organization can’t get out of the downward spiral that it’s been in over the last two decades is that there has been no stability when it comes to the head coach and general manager. Granted, the Raiders didn’t have a true GM until Reggie McKenzie was hired in 2012, but it’s not like Mark Davis has been patient with his decision-makers. To be fair, McKenzie got seven years. But even he had a few dud offseasons before putting together the 2016 roster, which has been the franchise’s best team since making the Super Bowl over 20 years ago. To put it in perspective, the Raiders were 10-37 during McKenzie’s first three years. Then, he had a great draft in 2014 (Khalil Mack, Derek Carr and Gabe Jackson), signed some quality free agents (Rodney Hudson, Kelechi Osemele and Michael Crabtree), and hit on his 2015 first-round pick (Amari Cooper) to put together a quality roster. The problem was that 2017 was a major disappointment, so Davis fired Jack Del Rio and hired Jon Gruden, which essentially stripped any power away from McKenzie and led to his firing a year later. In stepped Mike Mayock for three seasons until Gruden’s email scandal led to another leadership turnover, where Davis brought in the Josh McDaniels-Dave Ziegler duo for a season-and-a-half. That didn’t work out, so it was Tom Telesco’s turn for a year, only for Tom Brady to come in and hire Spytek. At some point, the Raiders have to stick with a plan and ride it out, even if the road gets bumpy. General managers — especially ones taking over bad teams/rosters, which is the majority of them — get hired because of the long-term plan they present to the owner, which typically is a three- to four-year vision. However, Davis hasn’t given a GM three seasons since Mayock, who was hired pre-COVID, and McKenzie is the only one of the five GMs Davis has hired to get four or more years! Do I think it’s fair to say Spytek should face criticism and feel a lot of pressure right now? Absolutely. But this franchise needs stability, and firing a third general manager in five years would be a mistake. The other…

title: Miami Dolphins offensive line review: Tracking the guards in Week 7
summary: Do my eyes deceive me, or did the Dolphins just win their first game of the Hafley/Sullivan era? Doing it against the Jets is an added bonus, but while wins and losses matter, much of the focus in 2026 remains on the development of Miami’s young talent. That is especially true along the offensive line, […]
full_text: Do my eyes deceive me, or did the Dolphins just win their first game of the Hafley/Sullivan era? Doing it against the Jets is an added bonus, but while wins and losses matter, much of the focus in 2026 remains on the development of Miami’s young talent. That is especially true along the offensive line, where rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea are important pieces of the team’s future. How are they performing this season? Each week, we take a closer look at the guards and what is being said about their most recent performance. Kadyn Proctor Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 1 71.2 79.0 63.4 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 2 62.0 72.4 39.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 57.5 51.1 71.3 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 51.2 48.6 64.9 10/11, vs. Bengals 66 (100%) 0 72.7 74.9 52.2 BYE 10/25, @ Jets 65 (100%) 0 59.6 58.2 61.3 Jonah Savaiinaea Game Snap Counts Penalties PFF Overall Grade PFF Run Blocking PFF Pass Protection 9/13, @ Raiders 59 (100%) 0 47.6 50.9 38.2 9/20, @ 49ers 56 (100%) 0 65.9 68.5 46.1 9/27, vs. Chiefs 73 (100%) 0 56.6 58.4 47.5 10/4, @ Vikings 39 (100%) 0 49.5 44.6 77.5 10/11, vs. Bengals 18 (27%) 0 45.4 44.7 78.4 BYE 10/25, @ Jets 65 (100%) 0 49.4 53,5 31.4 What We Learned The last time we looked at the guards, we were concerned over Jonah Savaiinaea’s ankle injury. With the extra week of rest, he was fine to play – but now we’re worried about Kadyn Proctor. Proctor has been ruled out for Week 8 against the Patriots due to a concussion, which hurts the team’s efforts to secure their second consecutive win and interrupts Proctor’s development. So far this season, the offensive line has been one of Miami’s biggest strengths, paving the way for five consecutive 100-yard rushing performances, and individually Proctor has yet to surrender a sack through six games. Proctor will likely be replaced by Jarrett Kingston, who filled in admirably during Savaiinaea’s injury in Week 5. Looking at the two guards’ PFF grades for this week, you wouldn’t think the Dolphins as a team had played especially well. Neither player earned a PFF grade of 60, generally considered league average, despite the Dolphins scoring four offensive touchdowns and controlling the game on the ground when it mattered most. That disconnect speaks to the difference between evaluating individual assignments and evaluating the offense’s overall success. Grades notwithstanding, the eye test reinforces what we’ve seen so far this year: Proctor is already an offensive force to be reckoned with. Physically, the athletic ability, power, and movement skills are already NFL-caliber: Locked On Dolphins’ Kyle Crabbs called Proctor’s performance against the Jets “ his best graded game of the season by a fairly comfortable margin.” There’s still room for growth, but the biggest opportunities are mental: recognizing defensive looks more quickly and becoming more consistent with his assignments. For Savaiinaea, it seems like he is still making progress and is light years ahead of where he was a year ago, but Proctor’s development appears to be further along at this stage (something the PFF grades would attest). He’s more consistently doing the things you want to see – washing defenders down the line, keeping his feet moving, not getting distracted by unexpected movements by the defense. He still played hesitantly at times against the Jets, which feels normal in the course of offensive line development. What is very clear on tape is that both Proctor and Savaiinaea were instrumental in Miami’s success on the ground. Time and again, they displaced Jets defenders and created cutback lanes for Ollie Gordon. More importantly, when the Dolphins needed to salt away the game in the fourth quarter, the coaching staff trusted the offensive line to win at the point of attack. That may be the most encouraging sign of all. The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor’s and Savaiinaea’s performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith’s film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins .

title: Dolphins fan confidence rockets to near all-time high in Week 8; Patriots game looming
summary: The Miami Dolphins, 1-5, beat the New York Jets in Week 7, putting together a complete performance in every aspect and looking like a team that can compete on any Sunday. The team is still in the midst of a complete roster rebuild, and it will continue to make the mistakes expected of the league’s […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - OCTOBER 25: Ollie Gordon II #0 of the Miami Dolphins scores on a 1 yard run during the first half of the National Football League game between the Miami Dolphins and the New York Jets on October 25, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, NJ. (Photo by Joshua Sarner/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins, 1-5, beat the New York Jets in Week 7, putting together a complete performance in every aspect and looking like a team that can compete on any Sunday. The team is still in the midst of a complete roster rebuild, and it will continue to make the mistakes expected of the league’s youngest team, but its potential was on full display last weekend. This weekend, the Dolphins face their second straight AFC East rival, this time hosting the New England Patriots. Miami hopes to back up its Week 7 win as it heads into Week 8, while the Patriots hope to avoid back-to-back losses for the first time this year. New England, 4-3, fell to the Chicago Bears on Thursday night to start Week 7, giving them 10 days to sit with the loss. The Patriots are hoping to stay within reach of the division-leading Buffalo Bills, who are 5-1 to start this year. According to FanDuel Sportsbook odds , the Dolphins are seven-point underdogs as the Patriots come into Hard Rock Stadium. Dolphins fan confidence Each week of the season, we use our SB Nation Reacts survey to gauge fans’ confidence in the Dolphins’ direction. Despite the team starting the season with five straight losses, Dolphins fans recognized the situation this season and accepted that Miami is a rebuilding team. The fan confidence survey has averaged around 75 percent positive responses throughout the year, hitting a low of 63 percent in Week 2 and a high of 87 percent in Week 5. Fan confidence in the team after their Week 7 win did not just rise; it leaped to a near all-time high. In Weeks 4 and 11 of the 2022 season, 99 percent of fan responses indicated they felt positive about the Dolphins’ direction. After Miami’s win last weekend, the 2026 fan confidence survey jumped from 72 percent in Week 7 to a new season-high of 97 percent in Week 8. What will happen on the field this week at Hard Rock Stadium? Will fan confidence in the Dolphins’ direction keep rising? Miami Dolphins 2026 Season Fan Confidence Results: Preseason – 80% Week 1 – 79% Week 2 – 63% Week 3 – 65% Week 4 – 79% Week 5 – 87% Week 6 – 71% Week 7 – 72% Week 8 – 97% Dolphins fans: Make your pick in the SB Nation app! Take Reacts surveys, create Dolphins polls, and see how your answers compare with fellow Phinsider readers. Then discuss the results with other diehard Fins fans. Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Win total Now that the Dolphins have their first win of the season, the next logical question is how many games they can win this year. We used the SB Nation Reacts survey to ask fans for their thoughts on Miami’s win total for the year. The preseason win total for Miami had been 4.5 games. Fans still think the Dolphins will land on the under side of that line, but they do think the Dolphins will come away with a few more wins over the remaining 11 weeks of the season. Asked whether the Dolphins will finish the season with 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5+ wins, three victories received the most votes, with 39 percent of responses. Four wins received 28 percent, and 5 or more wins picked up 21 percent of the vote. Together, 88 percent of fans expect at least two more victories. Two wins received 8 percent of the vote, while remaining at one victory this season received 4 percent ofresponses. Do you agree with the Dolphins’ fan confidence poll results? Let us know in the comments.

title: 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 7
summary: Wait, what? Did the Miami Dolphins respond to arguably their worst loss of the season with their first win? On the road?  You bet your sweet bippy they did. And against the Jets too – if you tell me the Dolphins go 2-15 this season but sweep the Jets, I’d say, “You know, not so […]
full_text: Wait, what? Did the Miami Dolphins respond to arguably their worst loss of the season with their first win? On the road? You bet your sweet bippy they did. And against the Jets too – if you tell me the Dolphins go 2-15 this season but sweep the Jets, I’d say, “You know, not so bad.” Here are five more things I think I think following the Dolphins’ first win. They Did the One Thing Winning Teams Do If there’s one ultimate flex in professional football, it’s this: Running the ball to drain the clock and close out a close game. Everybody in the stadium knows exactly what’s coming: The defense knows, the crowd knows, the broadcast team knows, everybody knows. And it doesn’t matter – the winning team lines up and closes the game anyway. On Sunday, that’s unexpectedly what the Dolphins were able to do against the Jets. Late in the fourth quarter, the Jets scored a touchdown (Mason Taylor?! Again?!) to pull within three points. They then kicked off, hoping to force a stop and get the ball back to tie or win it. The old Dolphins would have played conservative, forcing the Jets to burn their timeouts but giving Gang Green the ball and a chance to win. But what did the new Dolphins do? 3:17 left, 1 st down, 14-yard run from Ollie Gordon. Jets timeout. 3:10 left, 1 st down, 7-yard run from Ollie Gordon. Jets timeout. 3:04 left, 2 nd down, 1-yard run from Ollie Gordon. 2:21 left, 3 rd down, 1-yard run from Ollie Gordon. Two-minute warning. 2:00 left, 4 th down, 2-yard run from Malik Willis. First down. Victory formation. I mean, it wasn’t pure dominance: They needed a two-yard pickup on fourth down to secure the win, whereas ideally you’d lock that in on second or third down. Still, if you want to talk about the growth of a young team, this is Exhibit A with a gold star. Malik Willis Showed Tangible Growth What a difference a bye week makes, eh? Let’s revel in the stat line: 14-of-21 passing 228 passing yards 2 passing touchdowns 0 interceptions, 0 fumbles 37 rushing yards 1 rushing touchdown QB rating of 130.7! So what caused the change? A good night’s sleep? Frank Thomas’ testosterone supplements?* Yes and yes. But also, maybe better decision-making and resource utilization. Instead of going for deep shot after deep shot, against the Jets Willis threw more passes that were short of the sticks, completing a season-high 67% of his passes and keeping the offense on schedule. He also involved his tight ends more, with TE Greg Dulcich leading the team in targets and a season-high 86 yards, and he clearly benefited from having No. 1 receiver Caleb Douglas back. Willis still has more questions than answers right now, of course. But after opening the season with just two touchdown passes against seven turnovers, Sunday felt like the first game that provided a legitimate reason for optimism. I’m eager to see how he performs against the Patriots. *And she’ll like it too! Caleb Douglas Continues To Change the Offense I’m old enough to remember when Jon-Eric Sullivan and Co. caught a lot of flak for selecting Caleb Douglas in the third round and 75th overall. And who knows, maybe time will prove the doubters right. But man, the Dolphins look like a different team with Douglas on the field. It’s not just the traits and production – it’s the game-day savvy that you might not expect from a rookie playing his third game. His biggest play was a long catch-and-run touchdown in the fourth quarter. Douglas recognized a blitz, adjusted his route, caught Willis’ pass, broke a tackle attempt from Minkah Fitzpatrick and raced to the end zone. He also refused to be intimidated when Fitzpatrick got in his face, which is exactly what you want to see from a young receiver. OK, fine, Douglas only has 9 receptions on the season. But when averaging more than 20 yards per catch, it’s fair to say he’s giving this offense a much-needed jolt. The Offensive Line and Running Game Deserve Real Credit When was the last time we had a truly physical offensive line and running game? The Ricky Williams era? I’m not discounting De’Von Achane’s remarkable season last year, but that felt due more to his own speed and elusiveness than a dominant offensive line. Sunday’s performance wasn’t just productive. It was physical. For years, Dolphins fans have begged for an offense that could impose its will rather than relying solely on speed and scheme. Against the Jets, we finally saw a glimpse of that blueprint. Consider: Ollie Gordon rushed 25 times for 103 yards and a touchdown Maybe more importantly, the Dolphins as a team ran the ball almost twice as much as they threw the ball Gordon ran with toughness and attitude, but let’s not forget the offensive line really brought their lunch pails and got to work. The closing sequence mentioned above doesn’t happen without a tough, committed offensive line. Proctor’s injury might be a setback, but if the o-line is starting to gel, it’s not unreasonable to think we may have more games like this in store this season. The Defense Delivered When It Mattered Most OK, it wasn’t perfect. You don’t give up two touchdowns to Mason Taylor and 100 yards and a touchdown to Omar Cooper (side note: Does anyone else think Cooper might be a thorn in our side for years to come?) and claim the defense was exactly on point. That said, when the game hung in the balance, the defense came through. We’re talking: Michael Taaffe’s interception Jordyn Brooks’ 9 tackles, including 2 tackles for loss Chop Robinson’s red-zone sack A goal-line stand that forced a field goal rather than allowing a game-tying touchdown There’s a lot to clean up, and the team definitely needs more talent in the defense as a whole, but they showed up when it counted. It’s a start. So it’s worth appreciating the moment for what it is: The first win of the Hafley era, on a Dolphins takeover of MetLife stadium, no less The first time the Dolphins led at halftime The first time the Dolphins led, period So: Have the Dolphins arrived? Ha! No. The team still had busted coverages, dumb mistakes and an offense that mysteriously disappeared for much of the second half. But for the first time all season, the Dolphins started fast, protected the football, produced explosive plays, responded to adversity, controlled the line of scrimmage and closed out a close game. You know, the things winning teams do. In other words, they spent an afternoon looking a lot like the kind of team they’re trying to become. It’s worth celebrating.

(Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins claimed Jamree Kromah off waivers on Saturday, adding the former Chicago Bears edge rusher to the team’s 53-man active roster. To make roster space, the Dolphins waived edge rusher Robert Beal, Jr. Kromah began his NFL career as an undrafted free agent whom the Bears signed in 2024. He began his rookie year on Chicago’s practice squad before signing with the New England Patriots shortly after the start of 2024. He was waived a monthly later, returning to the Bears’ practice squad. He then spent 2025 on Chicago’s practice squad before making it to the active roster for 2026. He was waived this week after the Bears acquired defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons in a trade. He has appeared in two games, recording two tackles. Beal played in two games with the Dolphins this season, his first in Miami after three seasons with the San Francisco 49ers. He has one tackle. Kromah joins Chop Robinson, Josh Uche, Malik Herring, and Rodney McGraw as Miami’s edge rushers. The Dolphins face the New England Patriots on Sunday. Kickoff is set for 4:25 p.m. Eastern.

full_text: Before their NFC North clash with the Detroit Lions, the Minnesota Vikings have made a final move to solidify their roster. The team has announced that they have elevated running back DeeJay Dallas to the active roster ahead of Sunday’s game. This is the third elevation of the year for Dallas, so if the Vikings want to have him available going forward, they will have to sign him to the 53-man roster. He was elevated ahead of the regular-season opener against Green Bay and was also elevated ahead of last week’s game against Indianapolis. Dallas has been on the Vikings’ roster for all seven of the team’s games this season. In addition to his three elevations from the practice squad, he was on the 53-man roster for four games after the team signed him after they placed Jordan Mason on IR for his thumb injury following the season opener. When Mason was brought back ahead of the Colts game, the team released Dallas and immediately re-signed him to the practice squad. For the season, he’s carried the ball three times for ten yards, and caught four passes for an additional 34 yards. That will do it for roster moves for the Vikings ahead of Sunday’s game. We’ll have our Open Thread for Week 8 dropping at 11:30 AM Central, and we hope that you’ll join us for all the action!

full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on during the national anthem before the game against the Indianapolis Colts at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL’s last undefeated team has a problem , and it’s the same one that’s haunted Minnesota since Kirk Cousins tore his Achilles in 2023: quarterback stability. On this episode of Two Old Bloggers , Darren Campbell and Dave Stefano dive into the “Murray Bind” — the uncomfortable reality that Kyler Murray’s underwhelming play through six games has the Vikings staring down another offseason of quarterback uncertainty. “Murray’s play is once again setting the Vikings up to be in quarterback purgatory in 2027,” Campbell warns, citing Murray’s 89.3 QB rating and three touchdown passes in four full games. Meanwhile, NFC rivals are loading up: Quenton Nelson to Seattle, DeForest Buckner back to San Francisco, and Jeffrey Simmons to Chicago. The Vikings? Crickets. Dave Stefano laments, “Nolan Teasley grew up under John Schneider. And watching John Schneider get Quenton Nelson makes my heart break.” Key points from the episode: The Murray Bind : Through four full games, Murray has just three TD passes and 197 passing yards per game — not the resume that screams “multi-year extension.” With 11 games left and no franchise tag available, time is running out for the Vikings to gather enough data. Trade deadline inactivity : While rivals swing for the fences, the Vikings stand pat. Drew Bunting argues, “They are the epitome of one player away, aren’t they?” Names like Maxx Crosby, Jalen Carter, and Jonathan Taylor float as potential targets. Justin Jefferson’s disappearing act : The best receiver in football ranks 70th in catches and 44th in receiving yards. Bunting unleashes: “Start using them, jackass. Start throwing them the ball.” Jefferson hasn’t been targeted 10 times in a single game yet. 6-0 scrutiny : The Vikings’ opponents are 17-25, but Campbell notes the Bills’ opponents are 16-24 and the Chiefs’ are 15-25. “Why don’t they ask those teams who they have beaten?” Lions preview : Bunting calls this “the toughest game” of the November gauntlet, picking Detroit. His Shawshank-inspired battle cry: “I want him found now.” The keys? Win the turnover battle (Vikings are 41-4 when they do), contain Jahmyr Gibbs, and — somehow — get Justin Jefferson involved. Listen: View Link Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: The offense must prove itself against a Lions team with a retooled offensive line and revenge on its mind. As Bunting puts it: “It’s a show-me game.” Will the Vikings answer the bell or expose their ceiling? Tune in to find out. Fan With Us! We have your Minnesota Vikings talk amongst the Two Old Bloggers , Darren @KickassblogVike , and Dave @Luft_Krigare along with our numbers guy, Drew Bunting. Join the conversation! title: Should the Vikings Trade for Jonathan Taylor?
summary: The NFL trade deadline is approaching in just two weeks- November 10th. NFC teams like the 49ers, Seahawks, and Bears are making deals to bolster their roster. Should the Minnesota Vikings be aggressive in doing the same? The Vikings are undefeated and a Super Bowl contender. That typically is a recipe for an aggressive acquisition […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts runs with the ball past Isaiah Rodgers #2 of the Minnesota Vikings to score a touchdown in the first quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL trade deadline is approaching in just two weeks- November 10th. NFC teams like the 49ers, Seahawks, and Bears are making deals to bolster their roster. Should the Minnesota Vikings be aggressive in doing the same? The Vikings are undefeated and a Super Bowl contender. That typically is a recipe for an aggressive acquisition approach to bolster the team for a deep playoff run. Past Super Bowl champions have made some key acquisitions ahead of the trade deadline, so it would make sense for Vikings GM Nolan Teasley to be aggressive in his attempt to do the same. And yet sometimes an aggressive mindset can lead to poor decisions. Overpaying for that missing piece that turns out not to be. Or paying more for a ‘‘brand name” player when your own “private label” player is about as good. And while the focus is on this season, taking on some contracts now could have negative consequences down the road, as can trading away draft capital. Winning a Super Bowl likely vindicates every decision, but anything short of that could bring more scrutiny to a new GM. Ultimately the best trades are for quality players that circumstances made available who weren’t available previously, can fill a pressing need at a reasonable price, and makes sense longer term if a multi-year contract is being acquired. But the Vikings are also in a situation where Kyler Murray, Isaiah Rodgers, Harrison Smith, Andrew Van Ginkel, T.J. Hockenson, Jalen Redmond, Blake Cashman, Aaron Jones, Jauan Jennings, Jordan Mason, Blake Brandel, Ryan Van Demark, Ivan Pace, Carson Wentz, Kyle Van Noy, Andrew DePaola, Jay Ward, Bo Richter, and Zemaiah Vaughn are all on expiring contracts. The last several may not take much salary cap to re-sign, Harrison Smith will retire after this season and the Vikings are unlikely to extend Aaron Jones, but the Vikings have only $37.7 million in cap space next year, assuming the salary cap goes from $301 million to $325 million in 2027. That ain’t much considering they need to sign a starting quarterback and extend at least a few others on deals that are likely to average around $10 million/year. Certainly there are ways to finagle the salary cap by pushing more cap into future years, and it seems highly likely the Vikings will push a lot more of Justin Jefferson’s $49 million in base salary next year into future years, but if the Vikings were to take on another $16 million contract next year- as would be the case with Jonathan Taylor, for example, that likely means not being able to extend at least one other key player. For the Vikings specifically, the Taylor conversation is less about money for ‘26 than it is the future money on his contract. Pay a premium at the RB position in ‘27 and ‘28, and you’re then having to make a bunch of real tough decisions with a ton of major roster questions (QB,… https://t.co/XCJsY5Sgfs — Alec Lewis (@alec_lewis) October 31, 2026 There is the possibility that the Vikings could acquire Taylor for $4.4 million plus up to $1 million in incentives this year, then cut/trade him next year if it doesn’t work out beyond that without incurring a further dead cap hit if they do so prior to February 19th, when his 2027 base salary becomes guaranteed. However, it looks like the compensation required to acquire Taylor is likely to be at least and 2nd and 3rd round pick in 2027, with the Colts looking to get a 1st round pick or equivalent to part with him. The Colts have already turned down a 2nd round pick plus an additional later round pick. The Colts already turned down a 2027 second-round draft pick plus an additional pick for RB Jonathan Taylor, making clear they’d want a premium to trade the face of the franchise. All the trade updates you can handle in The Sweep Insider Notebook: https://t.co/2eiMVV6AJ1 pic.twitter.com/FDIrQ5k9gc — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) October 31, 2026 It appears that the market for Taylor is heating up as well, with the Packers now emerging as a leading contender (along with the Vikings) as Josh Jacobs’ off-field issues re-emerge and the league once again reviewing his situation. Jonathan Taylor trade talks are reportedly "active and ongoing," with the Broncos, Seahawks, Vikings, Packers, and Giants mentioned as potential destinations. https://t.co/GxBswOhNvs — ProFootballTalk (@ProFootballTalk) October 31, 2026 The Packers are making a very strong push for Jonathan Taylor, especially knowing the Vikings have him as their top target as well. Green Bay is preparing to move on from Josh Jacobs in the near future, and Taylor would immediately jolt their offense. Potential trade framework:… pic.twitter.com/sLubcUG6Jn — Evan Sidery (@esidery) October 31, 2026 It could be, as the Colts play interested teams off against each other, that the price for Taylor becomes similar to that paid by the 49ers to acquire Christian McCaffrey a few years ago, which was a 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and following year 5th-round pick. Is Taylor Worth It? Taylor has been one of the better backs in the league since he entered the league in 2020, but his performance over the past few years has been more mixed according to PFF grades: But he’s been a bell-cow back who has remained productive every season: He hasn’t been as productive as a receiver, but he’s definitely a name that will draw defensive attention. The hope that with Taylor in the backfield, opposing defenses will be forced to Taylor will turn 28 in January, which is when production tends to drop more significantly for running backs in the NFL. There are exceptions- like Christian McCaffrey and Derrick Henry- but on average running backs begin a more significant decline at ages 28-29. That sets up the Vikings to be paying Taylor $16 million in 2027 and $18 million in 2028 in what could be declining years for him as a running back. It could turn out to be a classic overpay for past production unless Taylor beats the odds and is able to extend his prime. What About Jordan Mason and Aaron Jones? Aaron Jones has taken on a heavy load this past month while Mason was on IR with a thumb injury and has done admirably for his age in that situation. But Jones doesn’t really force many missed tackles anymore, even as he is generally able to get what’s blocked for him. And he’s simply not a back that strikes fear in opposing defenses anymore. Jordan Mason, however, has quietly been a top ten back the past couple seasons in terms of average yards per carry, averaging 5.2 yards per carry in 2024 with the 49ers and 4.8 with the Vikings last season. That has at least equalled that of Taylor over the past two seasons. Taylor has been the bell-cow, however, while Mason was first an elevated backup with the 49ers and then worked by committee with Aaron Jones last season. Mason may not be everything that Jonathan Taylor is or draw as much attention as Taylor would in the Vikings’ backfield, but he has been productive with the opportunities he’s had. And he has the advantage of not requiring the Vikings to trade half their draft capital next year to have him in the backfield. He could also be extended for roughly half of what Taylor’s salary cap hit would be in the next couple seasons, maybe less, depending on how productive he is the rest of the season. Bottom Line Jonathan Taylor is a tempting target for the Vikings as the trade deadline approaches. And all signs point toward the Vikings being active in trying to trade for him. But how much is too much to pay for Taylor? full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: T.J. Hockenson #87 of the Minnesota Vikings celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts during the fourth quarter of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Vikings defense has given up the least yards and points per game and are second in passing yards allowed per game given up. The Vikings offense has is 29th in passing yards per game, 12th in rushing yards per game, and 24th in points per game. The Lions defense is last in passing yards allowed per game, 12th in rushing yards allowed per game, and 26th in points allowed per game. Something has to give right? Will the Lions continue to pass the ball very well? Will the Vikings pass the ball better? I expect more passing this game from the Vikings but they might try to force the run to win the time of possession battle which would be good. Can the Vikings run the ball better? Which brings me to the Jonathan Taylor trade talks/proposals/etc. On October 20, 2022, the Carolina Panthers traded running back Christian McCaffrey to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for a 2023 second, 2023 third, 2023 fourth, and a 2024 fifth. Is Taylor worth that much? According to a “report” linked below, the Colts want a first for Taylor. Should Nolan Teasley trade a first round pick for Taylor right now? The answer is complicated IMHO. First some facts. The team is 6-0. They probably will get at least 4 more wins giving them 10 which should make the playoffs. I think they get more wins. That puts the draft slot from #20 to #32. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason are both free agents in 2027. The 2027 RB free agent class is average at best to below average. https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/free-agents/available/_/year/2027/position/rb There are some folks who are already believing that Teasley needs to keep his first round pick to draft a rookie QB or to package with future picks presumedly which likely could be another first if you are coming up from at least #20. You have teams like the Cardinals, Titans, Jets, Browns, and Steelers all possibly looking for a young QB. The current draft class is starting to not look as many predicted earlier (or last year during the draft cycle). Manning and Moore probably need to stay. Chambliss has no more eligibility. Mestemaker, Carr, Mensah, and Simmons all have eligibility left and it is unknown if they will come out. I am thinking that not many will come out with the amount of NIL money they could get. There are a lot of other factors as well but the Vikings are playing too well to be in position to get a QB without giving up more draft capital. The NFL free agent QBs do not look very good right now either. You will have Murray, Mac Jones, Rodgers (retiring), Justin Fields, Jacoby Brissett, Deshaun Watson, Anthony Richardson, and others. https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/free-agents/available/_/year/2027/position/qb I am thinking Teasley will go with a free agent QB and it probably will be Murray unless he gets worse or does not get better. The other option that most want is Mac Jones. Maybe they go that route? I would not be upset with that move. That could mean the team will need to use a high draft pick on a running back in the next draft. How many draftees will be as good as Taylor? I would be OK with this offer … 2027 first, 2027 fifth, 2028 a conditional fourth for Taylor (bumps to a 3rd if he gets 1400 yards and 70% of the snaps in 2027) and a 2028 sixth … this solves the RB issue for 2027 and they will have a QB. I know many will say forget that and pass on getting a back like Taylor which is cool. I would love the hear the alternatives though. The Vikings offense faces split-safety looks on 41.3% of their snaps which is designed to limit Jefferson. Split-safety coverage inherently forces a defense to play with a “light box” (six or fewer defenders close to the line of scrimmage). It would be riskier to do that against a back like Taylor. It makes too much sense to go get Taylor (if possible) to pair with Jefferson right now. A side note: I will say this about the Bears trading for Jeffrey Simmons by giving up two firsts. Would you rather have Simmons or Banks and Donovan Jackson?
