title: Report: “No way” the Jets trade Garrett Wilson in 2026
summary: Well, the Garrett Wilson-to-49ers hope that a (very) few of you have can come to an end. Adam Schefter reported Saturday that a well-placed source said there’s “no way” the Jets trade Garrett Wilson: Maybe it’s surprising to some that Wilson won’t be moved. It’s not surprising that any chance the 49ers had for him […]
full_text: (Photo by Sarah Stier/Getty Images) | Getty Images Well, the Garrett Wilson-to-49ers hope that a (very) few of you have can come to an end. Adam Schefter reported Saturday that a well-placed source said there’s “no way” the Jets trade Garrett Wilson: One well-placed source told ESPN this weekend that there is "no way" the Jets will trade Garrett Wilson by the NFL's Nov. 10 trade deadline, despite any interest from other teams. pic.twitter.com/tzyCeBabNS — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 31, 2026 Maybe it’s surprising to some that Wilson won’t be moved. It’s not surprising that any chance the 49ers had for him is gone—I doubt they’d even do a trade for a wide receiver, but there’s a lot out there to suggest otherwise. The 49ers have a banged-up wide receiver room. Deebo Samuel and Mike Evans missed last week’s game against the Atlanta Falcons, and De’Zhaun Stribling has been on injured reserve since Week 1. The thing is, Samuel and Evans should be back after the bye (hopefully), and Stribling is back in December. So Wilson, if he was actually acquired, would come to San Francisco with no knowledge of the offense and have to produce. Something Brandin Cooks had to do weeks earlier. So the 49ers give up draft picks for a player whose cap number will climb past $35 million in 2028. Many of us hope DeForest Buckner finishes his career in San Francisco; that’s no way to do it with those salary cap hits. And let’s not forget players like Dominick Puni are eligible for an extension in 2027—we know how guards get poached from the 49ers, and Wilson coming to the 49ers would make the odds of that happening again more likely. From a financial and personnel perspective, it just doesn’t make sense to make a trade for Wilson. Yes, I say this crossing my fingers that the substation has moved on to other positions to injure. However, even if the 49ers manage to get a deal done, he’s still unfamiliar with the offense and has no time to build chemistry with Brock Purdy. Maybe he does it in a day? Maybe he takes until February? I don’t know. We don’t know who this source is: someone inside the Jets organization? Someone around the league? An agent? So we don’t know where the “no way” comes from. Whether the Jets have too high an asking price, are too dysfunctional to get it done in time, or no team wants to trade for that contract. Without context, we can only take this at face value, and “no way” means “no way” Now there is good in this for the 49ers. This also means some NFL squad in contention for an opening at productive wide receiver can’t get Wilson either. Which means he can’t be a problem for the 49ers defense later on. Wilson will stay with the New York Jets, and the Jets will…do Jets things.

title: DeForest Buckner joins growing list proving 49ers don’t burn bridges
summary: Dre Greenlaw, Deebo Samuel, Kendrick Bourne, and now DeForest Buckner. The San Francisco 49ers now have four players who left, either in free agency or via trade, and eventually made their way back to Santa Clara. You might see one or two players return to their original team, but not at the rate the 49ers […]
full_text: MIAMI, FLORIDA - FEBRUARY 2: DeForest Buckner #99 of the San Francisco 49ers stands on the sideline before the game against the Kansas City Chiefs in Super Bowl LIV at Hard Rock Stadium on February 2, 2020 in Miami, Florida. The Chiefs defeated the 49ers 31-20. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Dre Greenlaw, Deebo Samuel, Kendrick Bourne, and now DeForest Buckner. The San Francisco 49ers now have four players who left, either in free agency or via trade, and eventually made their way back to Santa Clara. You might see one or two players return to their original team, but not at the rate the 49ers have. There are two ways to look at this. The first is that the 49ers are a first-class organization. While wide receiver Mike Evans wanted to play with Brock Purdy , George Kittle sold him on it with all the things the 49ers do differently . It was either more modern technology, personalized nutritionists instead of a team nutritionist, or other small things that cost a lot of money and don’t show up on a salary cap sheet. The second: the grass isn’t always greener elsewhere. That’s not to say there aren’t grievances from the 49ers’ returning players. Dre Greenlaw had some choice words for Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton, but it’s not so much an indictment that other teams are worse, just that the 49ers do something right. Greenlaw left for a three-year, $35 million deal in Denver. This resulted in eight games and a release after one season. A r elease he felt was handled poorly . Then there’s Samuel. He was traded to the Washington Commanders and got a crowd-pleasing 17 carries. This is after he averaged around 45 a season over his previous four years with the 49ers. Same player, different usage. The time away was so short that Samuel said he felt like he never left . And finally, Buckner. The latest addition of returning players . The Chicago Bears were reportedly interested in the defensive tackle in this week’s NFC arms race. Buckner himself wanted San Francisco . Reports said Buckner was unhappy with the extension offer —which is fair. If there really were burned bridges back in 2020, would he really be gunning to go there? Doubtful. And that second point is even more valuable for rookies to keep in mind when their contracts expire. Sure, they can go for the big money—and they should—but they also now have three players in the building (minus Bourne, who returned for 2025 only) who went after a better deal or a different role and know what it’s like to leave the 49ers—sometimes frustrated. This isn’t an argument to say players need to take whatever cheap deal the 49ers offer because they are the 49ers. Sometimes letting players go is the 49ers’ mistake. While the 49ers used the savings from Buckner’s deal to extend Arik Armstead and Jimmie Ward, the trade itself—a first-rounder from the Indianapolis Colts—backfired because Javon Kinlaw—the pick meant to replace Buckner—did not work out. It’s helpful for veteran leadership and a talking point for the younger players. The 49ers have had some good drafts both in 2025 and 2026, and those young players can look to three people in the locker room who were drafted by the 49ers, left, and returned—and know what leaving the team is like as well as why they came back. Then they can look to George Kittle, among others, as to why he stayed. It also offsets the grievances of one Brandon Aiyuk. Aiyuk’s offseason antics of never wanting to do business with the 49ers create an impression of an insufferable organization. One that all players should avoid. And players talk; they take notice. Free agents and draft prospects can all look at Aiyuk and think something is wrong with the 49ers. Aiyuk looks more and more like a severe minority when you see Buckner, Greenlaw, and Samuel coming back and playing hard. Playing devil’s advocate for his side of the 49ers feud gets more and more difficult when you see other players having no problem returning—even after the 49ers couldn’t pay them what they wanted initially. If the 49ers were such an evil organization, how can you explain all three of them coming back? Again, Buckner said it was San Francisco or nowhere. I’ll never argue against a player getting paid. There’s too much fine print in a contract in a league referred to as “Not For Long” for them not to get the best deal for them and their family. That said, the fact that the 49ers keep the door wide open should they want to return—and players accept—says something about the organization. And the players themselves can tell rookies and second-year players what to expect when they sign on the dotted line with another team. Sometimes that’s more valuable than a film breakdown.

title: Five Washington Commanders players key to beating Eagles
summary: The Commanders have had another brutal, draining week in a season full of them. The news that defensive tackle Daron Payne suffered a season-ending foot injury on Friday was a hard to take, especially after so many injuries to big-time players.   In addition to dealing with that injury,Washington formally put Terry McLaurin on injured […]
full_text: The Commanders have had another brutal, draining week in a season full of them. The news that defensive tackle Daron Payne suffered a season-ending foot injury on Friday was a hard to take, especially after so many injuries to big-time players. In addition to dealing with that injury,Washington formally put Terry McLaurin on injured reserve, had a little dustup with Odafe Oweh talking about coaching , and essentially has its season on the line heading into Sunday night’s clash with the Philadelphia Eagles. I mean, come on. The Commanders must find a way to rally and go get a win over Philly that Amik Robertson essentially guaranteed . That means the Commanders must look to some key players to raise their games or assume bigger roles in order to lead Washington to victory. Here are five Commanders (not named Jayden Daniels) to watch in this Week 8 clash. WR Antonio Williams This one probably falls in the “Well, duh” category. Head coach Dan Quinn made it clear that Antonio Williams would see more snaps, largely working from the slot, with McLaurin now gone for the remainder of the season. They’ll need a big night from the third-round rookie, especially if Treylon Burks – he’s questionable – can’t go. Williams showed out against the Eagles in Week 1, with some of his best plays as a pro. Washington needs Williams to be efficient with his targets and create the separation required to get chunk yardage after the catch. DL Charles Omenihu The Commanders defensive line will play without Payne for the rest of the year. This week, they’re also working without Javon Kinlaw, who was ruled out with a knee injury. A position group that had been super deep and impactful, against the run, especially, is now being test. Johnny Newton is working to return from injured reserve , but he was formally ruled out of this game on Saturday afternoon. That puts a lot on Charles Omenihu’s shoulders despite the fact he, too, has been dealing with injury. He has been a solid pass rusher and a good player overall this season, but will probably see tons of snaps on Sunday night. They’ll need to be good ones considering how many defensive linemen are currently out. LB Sonny Styles With Jalen Hurts out for the season, the Eagles are using Tanner McKee at quarterback . The backup has, well, not been great . He could also prove vulnerable to making a game-changing mistake, whether it’s a bad decision or an errant throw. Styles is the type of athlete who can capitalize on those types of things. He has been impactful creating turnovers by punching the ball free or picking off a pass, with solid coverage and sure tackling, even if there’s room to grow as a blitzer. Styles has been on fire lately, with 26 tackles in his last two games. He’s a true sideline-to-sideline guy, and the Commanders will need him to be a force all over the field on Sunday. RG Sam Cosmi Putting an offensive lineman on this list doesn’t always made for a fun read, but Sam Cosmi is going to be huge in this one. While the Eagles are in shambles, their defense still features Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis and Moro Ojomo. Cosmi must lead a strong effort from the interior line overall to keep pressure off of Daniels and to create some interior rushing lanes to get the ground game going. Cosmi is one of the best in the business and can control his matchups. He has been solid working with Josh Conerly on the right side, which should be where most of the designed runs go. RB Rachaad White White was on this list last time in the game against the 49ers, as the Commanders tried to keep the run game going with Bill Croskey-Merritt on injured reserve. He responded with 27 yards on seven carries , plus four catches for 30 yards and a key touchdown against San Francisco. The Commanders need more of a steady rushing presence than that, with the carry total significantly higher, even with a by-committee approach involving Austin Ekeler and Jeremy McNichols. White must produce a solid start to the game as the Commanders try to assert dominance on the ground. If the Eagles pack the middle, then White’s work as a receiver can help keep the Commanders on schedule and into more manageable third downs than they have been creating so far this season. Who else should be on this list of Commanders that are key to victory? Let us know in the comments below:

full_text:
The spooky season is here, and the NFL uniforms are looking scary good in Week 8. The Jacksonville Jaguars and Detroit Lions lead the way as they debut their respective Rivalries combinations. 

 

 Jacksonville's look is nicknamed "Bold City," and the team will wear the uniform against the Indianapolis Colts , who debuted their own "Rivalries" design in Week 3 . The uniform includes a teal-glossed helmet with a gold face mask and "904," Jacksonville's area code, on the front and "Duuuval," the team's rallying cry, on the back. The white jerseys include black numbers and "Jaguars" in cursive. They both feature gold trimming, while the numbers have a teal shadow and jaguar-print pattern. A similar pattern appears on the black pants, which also have a teal stripe that includes gold trim running down the side. One neat detail is the names of Jacksonville neighborhoods hidden within the spots on the pants. 

 Detroit's "Defend the Den" threads will be worn vs. the Minnesota Vikings . The Lions' all-silver combination has various details with a message, including italicized black numbers that lean forward, meant to create the illusion of motion. The shoulder sleeve design of Honolulu blue meeting black mimics the gaze of a lion when it eyes its prey. The same appears as a pant stripe on the uniform's bottom half. And of course, Detroit's iconic car and racing culture are represented. The Honolulu blue lid's Lions decal is in carbon fiber black as a way to connect to that culture.

title: Ranking the top 10 trick plays in Super Bowl history
summary: Which trick plays cemented their legacies in the Super Bowl? We listed 10 that changed momentum or flat-out won championships.
full_text:
The Super Bowl is the biggest stage in American sports. Millions of people tune in to see the final two teams remaining from the NFL playoffs.

 It's the perfect time for a coach to dig into his bag of tricks and give his players a chance to do the unexpected. But it's also a high-risk, high-reward decision. If it goes right, the coach is a genius, but if it doesn't, his decision will be questioned forever.

 

 Dialing up a trick play at just the right time can catch the opponent slipping and lead to a huge momentum shift, such as Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Nick Foles catching a touchdown pass that led to an upset victory over the New England Patriots . It could also put a game out of reach, such as quarterback Phil Simms' flea-flicker pass to Phil McConkey that put the New York Giants two scores ahead of the Denver Broncos .

 Here are the 10 most memorable trick plays in Super Bowl history:

 COUNTDOWN TO SUPER BOWL LXI: ESPN will televise the Super Bowl for the first time in February. We are counting down to the big game with a Super Bowl Top 10 series, featuring rankings on everything from best catches and performances to biggest upsets, that will run every other Sunday leading up to Super Bowl LXI on Feb. 14, 2027. 

 

 

 1. Philly Special 

 When: Super Bowl LII -- Feb. 4, 2018

 Team: Philadelphia Eagles

 Opponent:  New England Patriots

 Situation: The Eagles were leading 15-12 in the second quarter and facing fourth-and-goal at the 1-yard line.

 Philadelphia desperately needed to answer the Patriots' touchdown, which trimmed New England's deficit to 15-12. Eagles coach Doug Pederson went for it rather than kick the field goal. Coming away with anything less than a touchdown going into halftime, leading by three points, would have been a deflating result for the Eagles, considering New England got the ball back to start the third quarter.

 "When you're playing the Patriots and Tom Brady, field goals don't win games," Pederson said after the game.

 Pederson called a timeout to talk things over with quarterback Nick Foles, who uttered the now-famous words, "Do you want Philly, Philly?" Foles was originally lined up in a shotgun formation before walking to the right side of the offensive line, next to tackle Lane Johnson .

 Jason Kelce snapped the ball directly to running back Corey Clement , pitched the ball to tight end Trey Burton as Foles leaked to the back of the end zone. Burton lofted the pass to a wide-open Foles to put the Eagles up 22-12 at halftime. Philadelphia went on to win 41-33 to secure the first Super Bowl victory in team history.

 

 

 2. "Ambush" onside kick 

 When:  Super Bowl XLIV -- Feb. 7, 2010

 Team: New Orleans Saints 

 Opponent: Indianapolis Colts 

 Situation: The Saints were trailing 10-6 at halftime.

 Saints coach Sean Payton wanted to steal a possession from Indianapolis' high-powered offense, which was led by Hall of Fame quarterback Peyton Manning. The play, which was named "Ambush," called for an onside kick even though teams don't typically do so to start the third quarter.

 The Colts never saw it coming.

 Saints rookie punter Thomas Morstead executed the kick perfectly. Chaos ensued as both teams scrambled for the ball after it bounced off the hands of Colts receiver Hank Baskett. Saints safety Chris Reis recovered the football in the pile.

 "All week we had practiced that onside kick," Payton said. "I told those guys at halftime, 'You've got to make me look good here.' It was a good hit by Thomas, and our guys did a good job of showing a normal kickoff coverage look."

 Quarterback Drew Brees and the offense took over at their own 30-yard line and completed a 59-yard touchdown drive that was capped by a 16-yard pass to running back Pierre Thomas. The decision sparked the Saints to outscore Indianapolis 25-7 in the second half and win the game 31-17. It was New Orleans' first Super Bowl win.

 

 

 3. Antwaan Randle El's pass to Hines Ward 
 When: Super Bowl XL -- Feb. 5, 2006

 Team: Pittsburgh Steelers 

 Opponent: Seattle Seahawks 

 Situation: The Steelers were leading 14-10 in the fourth quarter and facing first-and-10 at the Seahawks' 43-yard line.

 With nine minutes left in the game, the Steelers were looking to throw the knockout punch to secure their fifth Super Bowl title. Coach Bill Cowher believed the Steelers could have success on a trick play that the offense worked on during the Friday practice before the game. The Steelers needed to get near midfield, perhaps just past the 50-yard line.

 Such a moment occurred at the perfect time for the Steelers to utilize the passing skills of receiver Antwaan Randle El, who was a dual-threat quarterback in college at Indiana. Randle El's eyes lit up when he heard the play call, too.

 The Steelers tricked the Seahawks by turning a pitch to running back Jerome Bettis into a reverse for Randle El that turned into a deep pass for fellow receiver Hines Ward. The outcome was one of the most memorable plays in Super Bowl history, a perfect connection from Randle El to Ward for a 43-yard touchdown.

 "Instinctively, it just took me back to being a kid on the playground," Ward said in a recent interview with ESPN. "You see me take, like, two or three hops into the end zone. I didn't know what to do, you know? And words can't describe scoring a touchdown in the Super Bowl. And being in Detroit, seeing the sea of black and gold, waving the Terrible Towel, words can't describe that feeling."

 

 

 4. Robert Newhouse to Golden Richards 
 When: Super Bowl XII -- Jan. 15, 1978

 Team: Dallas Cowboys 

 Opponent: Denver Broncos

 Situation: The Cowboys were leading 20-10 in the fourth quarter and facing first-and-10 from the Broncos' 29 yard-line.

 A takeaway by the Cowboys created the perfect opportunity for the offense to have some fun. After a fumble recovery by cornerback Aaron Kyle, the Cowboys started their possession at the Broncos' 29-yard line. The Cowboys' trickery began when quarterback Roger Staubach pitched the ball to the left to fullback Robert Newhouse. The Broncos' linebackers moved forward because the Cowboys had two pulling linemen in front of Newhouse. In perfect timing, Newhouse invited the Broncos toward him before he turned his hips and threw a pass that traveled 35 yards. Just as impressive as Newhouse's pass was receiver Golden Richards' leaping reception at the goal line. Richards outjumped cornerback Steve Foley for the ball and celebrated his highlight by high-fiving a few of his teammates.

 The moment was historic, too, as Newhouse was the first player who wasn't a quarterback to throw a touchdown pass in the Super Bowl.

 

 

 5. Phil Simms' flea-flicker to Phil McConkey 
 When: Super Bowl XXI -- Jan. 25, 1987

 Team: New York Giants

 Opponent: Denver Broncos

 Situation: The Giants were leading 19-10 in the third quarter and facing a second-and-6 from the Broncos' 52.

 Giants coach Bill Parcells had been known as a more conservative coach who didn't take many risks offensively. Parcells was looking to go up by three scores and let his defense close the deal. So he called for a flea-flicker to generate a big play.

 Simms took the snap and tossed the ball to running back Joe Morris, who tossed it right back. Simms looked downfield and saw McConkey running free and hit him for a 44-yard gain. McConkey caught the pass and got flipped as he was tackled at the 1-yard line. Morris powered his way into the end zone on the next play, pushing the Giants' lead to 26-10.

 The Giants went on to win 39-20. Simms was named Super Bowl MVP and became one of the first to use the phrase "I'm going to Disney World!" after winning the big game.

 

 

 6. Deon Figures' recovery 
 When: Super Bowl XXX -- Jan. 28, 1996

 Team: Pittsburgh Steelers

 Opponent: Dallas Cowboys

 Situation: The Steelers were trailing the Cowboys 20-10 in the fourth quarter.

 Even before the Steelers faced the Cowboys, Cowher had already made a bold…

title: NFL Week 8 betting guide: The value bets to make on lines, props and anytime TDs
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 8 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: find betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league. Also included are fantasy projection creator Mike Clay's top predicted anytime TD scorers for Week 8.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. Let's get into it.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 
 Jump to: 
 Bowen's favorite bets 
 Solak's plays  | Walder's props 
 Clay's TD projections 

 

 

 Bowen's favorite bets 
 Looking at the Week 8 slate, we'll start with my top game in Detroit, as  Jared Goff  and an explosive  Lions  offense face the blitz-heavy  Minnesota Vikings . I also have a total I like in the Cleveland Browns - Pittsburgh Steelers matchup, and let's hit on another two-team teaser. As always, I'll give also give you some props I like.

 

 
 Minnesota Vikings at Detroit Lions 
1 p.m. ET on Fox, Ford Field, Detroit

 
 The Vikings' low-volume pass game has lacked rhythm with Kyler Murray under center, which has resulted in declining numbers for Justin Jefferson . It's a better matchup Sunday versus a Lions defense allowing a league-high 291.8 passing yards per game. This is the game to isolate and scheme for Jefferson.

 However, the key in-game matchup to watch is Goff versus Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Goff is going to see consistent pressure from the Vikings, who own a league-high blitz rate of 69.9%. Overload fronts, plus A/B gap blitzes to dent the pocket, which limits Goff's ability to climb/step up in the pocket. But Goff has been really good this season versus the blitz, completing 72.7% of his throws (third highest) while registering a 79.4 QBR (fifth highest).

 My take? The Lions have enough answers to create manageable pockets, while giving Goff quicker reads (and timing throws). Detroit covers the three points at home (-120) .

 Jahmyr Gibbs receptions OVER 4.5 (-03) 

 What are your immediate counters to pressure from the Vikings? Throw screens. Yes, Gibbs will be asked to play a critical role as a blocker in pass protection versus Flores' defense, but the Lions can deploy him on screens and quick releases from the backfield to beat the blitz, too. Gibbs has five or more receptions in five or six games played.

 Browns at Steelers OVER 39.5 (-105) 

 I get why the total is lower in this one. Both teams rank in the top 12 of defensive scoring and yards allowed per game. Plus, the Pittsburgh offense has lacked consistent big-play ability in recent weeks. However, when these teams me in Week 4 in Cleveland, the total hit 51. Aaron Rodgers threw for 299 yards and three touchdowns, and the Browns rushed for 112 yards. The weather looks good for Sunday in Pittsburgh. Give me the over.

 Two team, 6.5-point teaser (-143): Indianapolis Colts at Jacksonville Jaguars (-3.5) and Los Angeles Chargers at Los Angeles Rams (Even) 

 

 We hit on a two-team teaser last week, so let's bring it back, starting in Jacksonville. The Colts are unloading talent as part of a rebuild, with both Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner leaving via trade this week. So, we'll take the Jaguars off the bye. And teasing the spread down to 3.5 points is more comfortable than a touchdown and a field goal.

 What changes could have the 0-6 Chargers made during the bye week to jumpstart their offense? I expect to see some improvement, with more rhythm in the pass game for Justin Herbert . That's a start. But getting the Rams to even money (down from a 6.5-point favorite) is the play here.

 Omar Cooper Jr . receiving yards OVER 41.5 (-114) 

 Since returning from an ankle injury in Week 6, the rookie out of Indiana has been schemed up in the New York Jets ' game plan, and he's making plays. Cooper has posted back-to-back games of 100 or more yards receiving with at least five receptions in each. Cooper is an explosive, power strider who can produce numbers after the catch, plus he can get loose down the field on shot-play throws (three catches of 48 or more yards in his last two games). With his big-play potential and steady volume, I like the over to hit Sunday versus the Las Vegas Raiders .

 Derrick Henry total yards OVER 90.5 (-114) 

 This feels like a big number given that Henry has posted 60 or fewer total yards in back-to-back games. But the volume is there -- 18 or more touches in every game played this season -- and Henry gets a positive matchup versus a Buffalo Bills defense allowing 120 total yards per game to opposing running backs. This should be a get-right game for Henry.

 Rhamondre Stevenson total yards OVER 70.5 (-115) 

 The Miami Dolphins are allowing 148.2 total yards per game to opposing running backs. While I'd like to see Stevenson's rushing efficiency improve (3.7 YPC), he has posted at least 71 scrimmage yards in three of his last four games, catching 11 passes for 141 yards during that stretch.-->

 

 George Pickens anytime TD (+100) 

 Pickens has scored a touchdown in two of his last three games, and he has matchup advantages versus the Arizona Cardinals defense. This unit has allowed a league-high 17 touchdown passes this season and gave up 23 receptions of 20 or more yards (tied for sixth most). The Cardinals also play a bunch of Cover 2 (36.2% of opponent dropbacks), so there will be opportunities to isolate Pickens on a safety this Sunday.

 Kyle Pitts Sr . anytime TD (+285) 

 Pitts, who is playing his best football of the season, has seen his usage elevate over his last three games. During this stretch, Pitts has posted five-plus receptions in three straight -- with at least one touchdown grab in each -- and he has seen a total of six red zone targets. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers ' ability to dial up zone pressure is a factor here, but that defense has also allowed an average of 5.7 receptions per game to tight ends this season.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Zay Flowers OVER 6.5 receptions (+112) 

 The Bills are one of the worst coverage teams in football, and the performance of WR1s against them is evidence to that point. In Week 2,  Amon-Ra St. Brown  had nine catches for 142 yards. In Week 5, Puka Nacua had a whopping 17 receptions for 138 yards. Even Tre Tucker of the Raiders (5 catches, 97 yards) and Romeo Doubs of the Patriots (6 catches, 58 yards) had big performances going up against Buffalo.

 I continue to be enamored with Flowers' usage in Declan Doyle's offense. He has lined up more in the slot this season than ever before, and the Ravens easily manufacture him quick touches on crossing patterns and in the screen game. Flowers has had at least eight catches in three of his last four games and, in the two games to start the season (five catches apiece), he was hampered by a hamstring injury. The Ravens are going to use him at a high volume in every game, but this Bills matchup is particularly ripe for plenty of targets.

 Flowers is also +145 to score a touchdown in this game. The Bills have given up 11 receiving touchdowns to wide receivers this season, more than any other defense in football. In fact, the Bills are coming off of their bye week ... and still lead the league in receiving touchdowns surrendered to wide receivers. I will be tracking both of these bets.

 Kyler Murray OVER 24.5 rushing yards (-104) 

 We might finally see the Vikings in a trailing game script, as they are 3-point dogs at Detroit this Sunday. This Detroit defense is also a pass-funnel unit…

title: Miami Dolphins WR Caleb Douglas rounding into form ahead of Pats matchup
summary: The rookie wide receiver has impressed Dolphins coaches with his production on and off the ball.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- It's been a while since Caleb Douglas was on the sideline.

 The Miami Dolphins rookie wide receiver, who played all 27 possible games at Texas Tech over his final two collegiate seasons, would have to go back to his two years at Florida to find an extended period of time when he did not play.

 So when he missed three games this season with an ankle injury, it was new territory for him.

 

 "It's not easy," Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said last week. "For some people, it might be easy. For some people, it's a challenge. There are some guys that can learn by watching; there are some people that actually have to learn by doing. So I think it's different with every player.

 "Ultimately, the more you can actually do it, the timing, the rhythm, getting comfortable back with the quarterback, but mentally, he has stayed sharp because he's been pretty efficient in practice. But again, you're talking about a rookie who hasn't played much football."

 Douglas returned in the Dolphins' win over the New York Jets in Week 7, finishing with 70 yards and two touchdowns on two catches. His highlight play came on a 63-yard catch-and-run touchdown in the fourth quarter that effectively put the game out of reach.

 But the third-round draft pick caught Hafley's attention with his work outside of his two scores, mainly the cleanliness of his procedural work despite the extended absence, and his effort in the run game.

 "Those are the things that you worry about, right?" Hafley said. "We didn't have any of those errors from him. And those are, a lot of times the rookies, as you saw early in the year, that's not exactly easy for them ... And then his physicality in the run game. I thought he took a big step from where he was to when I turned on that tape and the way he was fighting with DBs. I thought that was pretty cool to see.

 "And then obviously you had the one really good route in the red zone and then the catch and run down the sideline. Hopefully we'll get a chance to get him the ball more."

 The Dolphins ran for 156 yards last week, their fifth straight game with more than 100 rushing yards. On a team that's dedicated to running the ball, it's critical that the receivers are willing to block.

 

 "Blocking is 90% effort, 10% technique -- you got to want to do it," Dolphins receivers coach Tyke Tolbert said. "I just believe that it's all about want-to ... it's really about the effort and showing up for your teammates in the run game or letting somebody else catch the ball, turn and block the man covering you.

 "That's the easiest thing to do. We'll call it a flip and find. Got to flip and find somebody to block. It's a want-to and it's more effort than anything."

 Dolphins receiver Malik Washington executed the "flip and find" on Douglas' second touchdown catch, acting as a lead blocker as Douglas ran down the sideline -- which the rookie thanked the veteran for after the game.

 Douglas saw only three targets in last week's game, although he did manage to maximize them. When he wasn't getting the ball, he was focused on applying Tolbert's principles on the field.

 "Just making sure that my man doesn't make the play," Douglas said. "Because that does not feel good when your man makes the play and then you know it was an effort thing too. I could have stopped him from getting there."

 The Dolphins take on the New England Patriots this week (4:25 p.m. ET, CBS). In the game, Douglas might find himself matched up with Pro Bowl cornerback Christian Gonzalez , who has allowed 15 catches for 144 yards in 175 coverage snaps this season, according to NextGen Stats.

 Douglas called his matchup a "great opportunity" but was hesitant to make it anything more than what it is -- one of 11 matchups on the field at any given time.

 "Honestly, man, just another DB," he said. "Just got to go out there and just win my one-eleventh."

title: The Patriots are 18-43 all time in Miami. Here are keys to a Week 8 victory
summary: Former Patriots player and current TV analyst Logan Ryan details what he thinks New England needs to improve on vs. Miami.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Quick-hit thoughts and notes around the New England Patriots and NFL:

 1. Uncharacteristic Pats: When former Patriots cornerback and two-time Super Bowl champion Logan Ryan was preparing for the television broadcast of Sunday's game between New England and Miami ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ), one of the things that excited him most was to share his analysis of receiver A.J. Brown .

 He was ready to declare it "the A.J. Brown game," adding how he knows Brown's "mindset and mentality" from their time as teammates with the Tennessee Titans .

 But as often happens in the NFL, Ryan had to be prepared to pivot, a result of Brown having his knee flare up and not being able to finish Wednesday's practice before missing the rest of the week. 

 Brown was officially ruled out Saturday, along with running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness), which continues a season-long theme of managing the roster due to a relentless run of injuries.

 The game still remains very much in Ryan's wheelhouse because of his connections to both teams -- having played for Patriots coach Mike Vrabel in Tennessee, as well as alongside veteran New England safety Kevin Byard , and crediting Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley for hatching his NFL playing career after playing for him when Hafley was defensive backs coach at Rutgers.

 What stands out to Ryan about the Patriots from his film study?

 "I see a well-coached and balanced team with too many uncharacteristic turnovers [14, second most in the NFL]. I know that is not a Mike Vrabel team with the turnovers. And I see too many missed tackles defensively holding them back in terms of the next step in consistency," he said of a defense that has forced just seven turnovers.

 "Sometimes when chasing turnovers defensively, you miss tackles because you're not securing it first. I'm sure [Vrabel] continues to preach the fundamentals but it's an uncharacteristic kind of spell they've been in."

 

 New England's 34 missed tackles are 14th most in the NFL, just above the league average of 33.4 missed tackles per team, according to ESPN Research. They had a season-high 11 missed tackles against the Bears last week, but Ryan believes better results should come.

 He noted the 10-day stretch since that game, which provided more time to tighten things up, and he's curious to see how that manifests itself against a 1-5 team coming off its first victory of the season -- 28-25 over the Jets on the road.

 He also will be watching how much  Drake Maye  is on the run -- by choice or not -- and if the Patriots can bottle up quarterback Malik Willis as a rushing threat (223 yards on the ground, second most among QBs).

 "These are two of the top scrambling quarterbacks in the NFL and I'm not sure people understand how good Drake Maye (211 yards, fifth among QBs) is running and extending plays with his legs," he said.

 "Malik Willis, his calling card, he's a running quarterback and that can break the structure of a Vrabel defense. When a quarterback can get out and extend the play, it can break the discipline in a defense. It takes coaching out of the it and now it's more of a freestyle play."

 Ryan has another thought that could come up on the broadcast, and it's based on first-hand experience. The Patriots are 18-43 all-time in Miami.

 "Why do the Patriots often struggle in the heat?" he asked. "I've been a part of that myself."

 

 2. Hollins on the cusp: The Patriots ended the week with just three healthy receivers on the 53-man roster, but veteran Mack Hollins ' presence on the Week 7 trip to Chicago indicates he's progressing on injured reserve (calf). He's eligible to be designated for return after Sunday's game in Miami.

 At the time he was placed on IR, Hollins had led the team with 15 receptions and 209 receiving yards.

 3. Hafley-Vrabel link: Hafley coached Vrabel's son, Tyler, for three seasons at Boston College . As a result, he had a connection with Mike Vrabel, and now the two face each other for the first time as NFL head coaches.

 "I got to know him pretty well then. He was really good to me. We talked on the phone a lot if I ever had football questions, being-a-head-coach questions," Hafley said. "And he'd come and sit in the stands just like a normal fan. I appreciate how he has stayed in touch with me and how he's helped me along the way. And I just respect the way they play."

 

 4. Road warriors: The Patriots are 1-3 on the road after going 9-0 away from home last year. Regaining that edge has been a point of emphasis in a week in which players and coaches have said they don't view the Dolphins as a reflection of their 1-5 record.

 "This is a division game and you have to win on the road in this league. Last year, that was just a mentality and a mindset ... we want to do that [this year]," defensive tackle Milton Williams said.

 5. Weather prep:  Maye said one thing he's learned from his road games in South Florida, going back to college, is the importance of hydrating throughout the week and not waiting until game day.

 Meanwhile, Patriots kicker Andy Borregales , who grew up in South Florida, said the possibility of a delay for thunderstorms always is a consideration and has been on his radar with Sunday's 4:25 p.m. start. He said the key is staying in routine as possible and "rolling with the punches."

 6. Cap space: After entering the week with a league-low $1.5 million in salary cap space, the Patriots created $3.21 million in additional room by restructuring veteran tight end Hunter Henry 's recently-extended contact . That gives the team $5.245 million in space to help get through the season, which is needed to account for when players land on injured reserve and others are brought on to the roster. Also, the NFL trade deadline is Nov. 10 and the extra space could help take on a player with a modest contract.

 

 7. Champs' reunion: The Patriots will honor the 10-year anniversary of their Super Bowl LI team at next Sunday's home game against the Packers, which coincides with Rob Gronkowski's Patriots Hall of Fame induction the day prior (1 p.m., free to public) and Fox's Tom Brady in town to call his first-ever New England game.

 Ryan called that "one of the favorite teams" he played on, but he'll miss it because CBS has him calling the Browns-Saints game in New Orleans.

 8. They said it: "I got the bug. I'm a storyteller by nature and I'm trying to take all my tips and tricks as a player and call the game through a player's lens of what they're seeing and feeling. I hope someone turns on the game as a Patriots fan, and a Dolphins fan, and that you enjoyed it, learned something, laughed and had fun, because it's Sunday and we're trying to get away from real-world problems and watch the best sport." -- Logan Ryan, on transitioning into broadcasting 

 9. Elliss' timing: Starting Patriots linebacker and leading tackler Christian Elliss (51) smiled in the locker room when recalling how fortunate he felt that the team played on Thursday in Week 7, because he and wife Kaysie welcomed their fourth child, Tautua, three days later on Sunday, the usual game day. Tautua is Samoan and means "to serve."

 10. Did You Know : Henry leads the Patriots with 296 receiving yards, the fewest for the team's leading receiver through the first seven games in franchise history, according to ESPN Research. Patriots receiver DeMario "Pop" Douglas has a team-leading 18.7% target share and, since Hollins injured his calf Oct. 4, is tied with Henry for the club lead in receptions (14).

title: Will usually active Jets play or pass before trade deadline?
summary: New York could look to add to its pile of assets ahead of the Nov. 10 trade deadline.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- A look at what's happening around the New York Jets :

 1. Ready, set, trade: General manager Darren Mougey has executed 14 player trades in 14 months, so it's easy to assume he will be wheeling and dealing as the Nov. 10 trade deadline approaches. Don't be surprised if that's not the case.

 There won't be a sell-off like last year (see: Sauce Gardner and Quinnen Williams blockbusters). There might not be anything splashy. It feels like the Jets (2-5) are leaning toward standing pat. Of course, never say "never" with Mougey.

 Let's examine where the Jets stand regarding trade candidates.

 Wide receiver Garrett Wilson  generated the most buzz this week after frustration spilled into the media -- with him having to answer questions about if he wanted to be traded or not and ESPN's Adam Schefter reporting Saturday that there's "no way" that the Jets would deal their star wideout. Wilson told reporters that he won't ask for a trade despite his lack of targets in recent weeks amid the losing. Stay tuned, though. This could be an offseason storyline, especially if things don't improve.

 Braelon Allen 's emergence at running back has fueled speculation about Breece Hall , but would the Jets trade him six months after giving him a three-year, $43.5 million extension? It happened to Gardner last year. In this case, it seems unlikely.

 The Jets believe that they have the NFL's best 1-2 punch, and they don't want to break it up. Even if they wanted to move him, Hall's recent injuries may give teams pause. He has missed four games because of a quadriceps injury after missing a chunk of training camp because of a strained groin.

 More realistic trade candidates:

 
 Will McDonald IV : Remember when coach Aaron Glenn boasted about how they would coach him up, turning him into an all-around force? That was a year ago. The former first-round pick is now a part-time player with only two sacks and four quarterback hits. But he has pass-rushing ability (10.5 sacks in 2024), so there will be interest. Former Jets coach Jeff Ulbrich is the  Atlanta Falcons ' defensive coordinator, and he could use an edge rusher. McDonald, due a guaranteed $13.8 million in 2027, could bring back a fourth- or fifth-round pick. 
 Nahshon Wright : He told ESPN that he's frustrated and open to a trade, a sentiment he said he shared with the organization. It seemed to be a good signing at the time, a noted ballhawk (five interceptions last season with the Chicago Bears ) joining a team that had no picks in 2025. It hasn't worked out, as he has yet to play a defensive snap. He's on a one-year deal for $3.5 million. 
 Jarvis Brownlee Jr .: He was a healthy scratch last week because he missed multiple mandatory meetings , leading to a team fine, Brownlee told ESPN. He might be back in the lineup this week, but rookie D'Angelo Ponds is waiting in the wings at nickel back. Acquired in a September 2025 trade, Brownlee is on a team-friendly contract through 2027. 
 Andre Cisco : The veteran safety lost his starting job to Dane Belton in the preseason, reducing him to spot duty on defense and special teams. He's a four-year starter, still only 26, on a modest, one-year contract. Maybe a contending team, in search of safety depth, will come calling. 
 Jamien Sherwood : The linebacker won't be easy to trade because his contract has more than $4 million remaining this season, plus a non-guaranteed $15 million in 2027. At times, Sherwood has frustrated the organization, which gave him a three-year, $45 million deal last year. There was talk of reducing his role, but his play has improved over the past two weeks. 
 Harrison Phillips : He's a good locker room guy and a run-stuffing defensive tackle, but he's in the final year of his contract at age 30. The interior line is thin because of injuries, so it probably makes sense to hold on to him. 
 Tight end: They have more tight ends (five) than they know what to do with, so it wouldn't be a shock if one of them gets moved. Jeremy Ruckert and Jelani Woods (free agent in 2027) are the most likely candidates. 
 
 

 2. Conflicting agendas? There's an interesting dynamic as the trade deadline approaches.

 Presumably, Mougey has an eye on the future because that's what GMs do. Glenn, likely coaching for his job, needs as many wins as possible, so he'd be less apt to trade players for draft picks. This can be a slippery slope for teams when jobs are on the line. In this case, the sense is that Glenn will get a chance to flip the fortunes of the current roster, which isn't devoid of talent.

 3. What happens in Vegas ...  The Jets host the Las Vegas Raiders  (3-4) on Sunday, setting up one of those quirky matchups that we occasionally see in the current salary cap climate.

 Quarterback Geno Smith is receiving most of his salary from the Raiders, who traded him in March. The Raiders are paying $16.3 million, with the Jets responsible for the rest ($3.3 million).

 This is one of those cases in which a player can hand a loss to the team paying most of his salary.

 4. Wee-hour news flash: It's funny how news travels in a social media world. Cornerback Azareye'h Thomas said he received a 3 a.m. text from a family member passing along Ashton Jeanty 's eyebrow-raising comments about the Jets' defense. The Raiders' running back was critical, saying the Jets have a "couple of guys ... that don't really want to tackle."

 Publicly, Thomas and his teammates shrugged it off, but the quote was a topic of conversation behind closed doors, players said.

 

 5. Two hats : Glenn gave a candid answer when asked about his dual role, managing the game while calling the defense. He insisted it's not too much on his plate, but he acknowledged, "It's not easy. I'll be up front and tell you that."

 It's fair to wonder if it's contributing to the Jets' well-documented issues with clock management.

 6. Got a minute (or two?) : The Jets are devoting additional practice time to two-minute situations, according to Glenn. They do a two-minute jog-through on Wednesdays, a live two-minute period on Thursdays and another two-minute session on Saturdays.

 This has been an epic struggle. In 24 games under Glenn, the Jets have been outscored 107-6 in the final two minutes of the first half.

 7. Lucky horseshoe: When the Jets traded Gardner to the Indianapolis Colts for a package that included first-round picks in 2026 and 2027, New York didn't expect either of those picks to be very high. After all, the Colts were 7-2 at the time, looking like a team on the rise.

 Since then, they've lost 12 out of 15 games. The 2026 first-rounder turned out to be No. 16 (tight end Kenyon Sadiq ) and the 2027 first-rounder seemingly is improving by the day.

 The Colts have traded two of their best players -- guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner . More trades appear imminent, including being open to trading one of the NFL's most dangerous offensive players in running back Jonathan Taylor, sources told ESPN and NFL Network .

 It could work out brilliantly for the Jets. At 2-5, the Colts own the seventh pick, per Tankathon. The Jets also have their own pick (10th) and the  Dallas Cowboys ' pick (12th), giving them plenty of ammunition if they want to trade up for a quarterback.

 

 8. Where's Sadiq? The rookie has been invisible (four catches for 24 yards) since his seven-catch, 105-yard breakout in Week 3. What gives?

 Offensive coordinator Frank Reich said Mason Taylor 's return from injury has resulted in a lower target share for Sadiq, but he acknowledged, "We can do a better job of getting him a few touches here and there."

 They made him a first-round pick for a reason.

 9. Motown memory: Whenever things look bleak, Glenn occasionally references his previous team, the Detroit Lions , who reversed their fortunes in 2022. He hasn't brought this up publicly, but it might have crossed his mind.

title: How to bet Eagles-Commanders: Analysis, tips and top prop plays
summary: Odds, bets and analysis to help you bet the Philadelphia Eagles-Washington Commanders game Sunday night.
full_text:
The Washington Commanders ' blitz is the biggest problem for the Philadelphia Eagles . QB Tanner McKee has struggled when extra rushers come, and missing OT Lane Johnson makes protection that much tougher. I'd expect quick throws to TE Dallas Goedert and rookie WR Makai Lemon , giving McKee somewhere to go before pressure arrives. Goedert is the better matchup because Washington has struggled to cover tight ends. Philadelphia needs those completions to avoid third-and-long situations, especially with Saquon Barkley 's workload uncertain.

 

 For Washington, this starts with keeping Jayden Daniels comfortable. Philadelphia has struggled to generate pressure, and Daniels can attack downfield when he has time. Stefon Diggs , if available, can work inside against an Eagles defense that has struggled against slot receivers. Daniels' legs also punish defenders who turn their backs in coverage. Philadelphia needs disciplined rush lanes, forcing him to throw without opening escape routes. Neither offense handles third downs well, so winning early downs should decide who gets to dictate the game.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 

 I prefer Philadelphia with the points because Washington hasn't earned this much separation. The Commanders are allowing 28.7 points per game and have given up touchdowns on 18 of 22 opposing red zone trips. Philadelphia doesn't need a complete offensive turnaround to make a few scoring opportunities count.

 

 Washington's offense also converts just 30.9% of third downs, making me reluctant to assume it can build a lead and consistently extend it. Getting more than a field goal is beneficial when neither team has been dependable offensively.

 A bet on the over requires less of an offensive breakout than the low points total suggests. A 23-20 game gets there, and both defenses allow at least 25 points per game. But those averages aren't enough alone. Philadelphia's injuries could lead to promising possessions ending in punts. I see enough defensive weakness for the over to hit, but the Eagles covering feels like the stronger position .

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 Jayden Daniels passing yards OVER 203.5 (-111) 

 Pamela Maldonado: Philadelphia's pass rush, or lack thereof, is the reason. The Eagles rank last in sack rate and quick pressure, and opponents average 7.9 yards per attempt when they don't face pressure. Daniels has averaged 8.0 and 7.5 yards per attempt in two games since returning from his elbow injury. Diggs' availability matters because his slot matchup gives Daniels a reliable way to move the ball.

 

 

 Antonio Williams over 34.5 yards receiving (-111) 

 Matt Bowen: Williams could be in line to see more usage with Terry McLaurin (knee) now down for the season. The rookie caught three of four targets for 50 yards in the Week 6 loss to the Niners, and he has had three receptions in each of his past three games. With the route traits to uncover, plus the field awareness to find open grass, Williams can operate as an outlet for quarterback Jayden Daniels on Sunday night versus the Eagles' zone schemes.

 Dallas Goedert anytime TD (+230) 

 Liz Loza: Goedert was a spike machine last season, recording a position-high 11 scores in 2025. The complexion of Philadelphia's offense this go-around is, obviously, much different. Still, Goedert remains a focal point, averaging over six targets per game and ranking fifth at the position in red zone target share (30%). With DeVonta Smith sidelined, the veteran tight end figures to be heavily involved, particularly in the scoring area of the field. Washington's defense has surrendered the second-most TDs to the position (8), including a pair of TDs to Goedert himself back in Week 1.
